#5507. From Mold Poisoning to Lyme Disease: Inside the Extreme Moves 6 Stars Made to Save Their Health

In many cases, a health diagnosis can be life-changing. From dealing with symptoms to navigating treatment, managing medical issues is no easy feat.

And while accessibility upgrades and wellness integrations can certainly make a home more habitable in these instances, some people choose to pack up and move altogether—particularly celebrities.

Of course, celebrities may also have the means to relocate when particular symptoms could be managed more easily in a different climate.

Although some high profile individuals prefer to keep these kinds of decisions close to the chest, a handful of celebs have spoken candidly about the health-related circumstances that inspired them to migrate.

Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg recently offloaded their longtime Illinois residence for $2.6 million. The transaction comes just as “The Masked Singer” host has publicly shared her experience dealing with the effects of “mold and mycotoxin poisoning.”

During the Oct. 28 episode of “The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show,” she revealed that she’s been living in a tent after undergoing the costly experience of remediating her home.

In a later episode, McCarthy also noted that she has discarded all of her clothing and furniture in a continued attempt to escape the mold.

In the wake of the ordeal, she’s considering a relocation.

“I’m so paranoid that I’ve even talked to Donny about moving out of the midwest, where it’s humid, and going to a dry location like Vegas or Arizona or something, because my body just can’t detox mold very well,” McCarthy said.

McCarthy and Wahlberg have yet to make a permanent move, but the sale of their St. Charles property could certainly be the first step towards change.

Retired Major League Baseball star Matt Holliday and his wife, Leslie Holliday, were left with no choice but to leave the dream home they’d built in Stillwater, OK, when he was diagnosed with a respiratory disease.

“The doctor said he needed to get to dry climate quick,” listing agent Vincent Clark told the Phoenix Business Journal.

Clark is the agent representing the sale of the Paradise Valley, AZ property the Hollidays initially relocated to.

They purchased the $10.6 million home in February of this year after the World Series champion received the diagnosis a week after a water leak had affected their 136-acre custom home in Oklahoma, which is still on the market for $8.95 million.

While the sprawling Arizona property was well-equipped with “substantial healthy-home enhancements” including air and water filtration and conditioning systems, Clark revealed that the Hollidays are seeking a home with an existing guest house, although the 7,781-square-foot home they’re hoping to sell includes transferred approved plans for an 845-square-foot guest casita.

In an Aug.10 social media post, “The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives” alum Mikayla Matthews admitted that her “home situation is always up in the air.”

The reality TV personality was diagnosed with Chronic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (CIRS), which she believes was triggered by extended exposure to mold-related toxins.

She and her family spent much of 2026 traveling in hopes of easing her symptoms, and temporarily relocated to Hawaii in May before heading to Florida in June in pursuit of a humid climate.

“The heavy metals in the air from Great Salt Lake drying up add to my toxic load everyday, so I can’t detox everything out,” she wrote in an Instagram post.

In October, Matthews revealed that her family was leaving the home she says was “making” her “sick,” and had purchased a new home in Utah, which is still under construction.

Bella Hadid recently purchased an idyllic $5.5 million home in Colorado, but it’s not the first time she’s snapped up a property with a stunning connection to nature.

In 2024, the model spoke to Allure about her decision to take a break from the industry in pursuit of a more laid back lifestyle in Fort Worth, TX, citing mental health struggles including severe anxiety and brain fog, as well as her longtime battle with Lyme disease.

The move marked a focus on her mental and physical health, as well as a dedication to a passion she’d lost with fame: horseback riding.

At the time, Hadid was dating Adan Banuelos, an equestrian trainer. The pair were seemingly on and off for two years before separating earlier in 2026, but during their time together, she began competing in amateur cutting horse competitions after a history as a longtime show jumper.

Musician Taylor Dayne decided to trade a life in Los Angeles for a slower pace in Santa Barbara after recovering from stage two colon cancer.

The “Tell It To My Heart” singer considered the move to be part of her healing process.

“I loved the idea of living in this sanctuary. It’s pretty magical up here,” she said to the Montecito Journal. “I am really relishing being in a sacred space where everybody is pretty damn happy.”

Dayne told People magazine that she’s feeling healthy four years after her diagnosis in July of this year.

“So far, so good,” she said of her health. “All clean.”

Actress Jamie Lynn Sigler was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in her early 20s, and kept it private for nearly 15 years before revealing the diagnosis in 2016.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, “The Sopranos” star and her husband, Cutter Dyktra, left California with their two sons, Beau and Jack, and relocated to Texas.

“We needed a change. When I moved here, I started using a cane once in a while because I didn’t feel like I was being watched,” she told Us magazine. “Here, it was like, ‘I’m just Beau and Jack’s mom at the baseball field.’”

The mom of two has shared that her family is fully embracing their new life.

“I feel disconnected, in the best way I’ve ever known,” she told People magazine. “It’s all about outdoors and nature which I really appreciate since I never had it growing up in New York and L.A.”

#5505. Rajiv Ramaswami to step down as Nutanix begins hunt for its next CEO

Rajiv Ramaswami is stepping down from his role as chief executive of Nutanix Inc., six years after he joined the hyperconverged cloud infrastructure company from its rival VMware Inc.

In a letter to company employees, Ramaswami (pictured) said he’s going to continue in the role for the time being while he works with Nutanix’s board of directors to identify a successor and assist with the transition. “After that, I will continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time,” he said in the letter.

Ramaswami, who is 60 years old, did not give any reason for his coming departure, but the letter seems to indicate that he’s not ready to retire just yet.

“Our next CEO will inherit a strong platform, a loyal customer base and, most importantly, an exceptional team,” Ramaswami wrote. “Until then, my focus remains on leading this company and nothing about our day-to-day priorities changes. I am committed to helping our next leader succeed, and my ask of you, as always, is to continue to focus on executing as we go through this leadership transition.”

Ramaswami added that Nutanix has hired an executive search firm to lead the hunt for his successor. The news came as the company delivered its first-quarter earnings report, posting modest year-over-year gains in profit and revenue.

The company reported adjusted earnings of 73 cents per share, beating Wall Street’s target of 61 cents per share by a strong margin. Revenue for the period came to $772.4 million, up 15% from a year earlier and above the Street’s forecast of $762.7 million.

Nutanix’s outlook for the current quarter is strong, with the company guiding for sales of between $820 million and $830 million, compared with the Street’s consensus estimate of $820.4 million. However, the full-year picture is a little less rosy, with Nutanix guiding for annual sales of $3.18 billion to $3.23 billion. The midpoint of that range trails the Street’s forecast of $3.22 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue.

Investors did not take the news very well. The cautious full-year guidance compared with the uncertainty over leadership prompted many to sell, and Nutanix’s stock was down 8% after-hours, having already fallen more than 5% during the regular trading session, on a down day for many tech stocks.

Virginia Gambale, of the board at Nutanix, hailed the “tremendous impact” Ramaswami had on the company during his six-year tenure. “Rajiv led the company’s transformation to subscription software, built a loyal and expanding global enterprise base and established a technology portfolio that we believe positions us well for the AI era,” she said. “We’re focused on selecting an exceptional leader who can build on that foundation.”

In a conference call with analysts, Ramaswami said he believes the company is embarking on the third major chapter in its history. The first chapter, before his arrival, saw the company establish itself as the leader of the hyperconverged infrastructure industry. Chapter two began when he took over, and saw Nutanix expand from those roots to become a platform company, he said.

“[We have] transformed the company to be profitable while growing and expanding the product portfolio quite significantly, from HCI to a platform that works across clouds, supports external storage and has cloud-native capabilities and now moving into the future with AI capabilities,” Ramaswami said. “Chapter two is well-established at this point and there’s a lot of opportunity in terms of driving growth. I feel like we are in a very good place.”

According to Ramaswami, Nutanix now stands at an inflection point as it looks to cash in on the new era of artificial intelligence. “I’ve been talking to the board for a bit about this, as well as in terms of our strategic direction and the timing for succession, and so we came to the conclusion together that this is perhaps the right time,” he told analysts. “[We wanted] to announce it ahead of time as we look for the appropriate next leader.”

Ramaswami’s departure from the company should at least be a lot smoother than his arrival. Nutanix announced it had appointed Ramaswami as its CEO in late 2020, just two days after he quit his role as chief operating officer of its biggest rival, VMware.

VMware was indignant about the manner of his departure, and responded with a lawsuit that accused Ramaswami of breaching his legal and contractual duties to the company by “secretly meeting” with Nutanix’s board to discuss taking over, while continuing to play a leading role in shaping its product and business strategy. The lawsuit was ultimately settled out of court about a year later.

In April, Ramaswami appeared on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s mobile livestreaming studio, where he talked about how Nutanix is shifting away from HCI to focus on more of a “disaggregated infrastructure” strategy to support demand for autonomous AI agents:

#5504. ‘Selling Sunset’ Alum Emma Hernan Reveals How Her West Hollywood Kitchen Launched Her Food Empire

Before she ever became a luxury real estate agent at The Oppenheim Group or appeared on the Netflix hit “Selling Sunset,” serial entrepreneur Emma Hernan had hired Jason Oppenheim to help her buy a home in West Hollywood, where she has since launched several successful businesses.

The 1940-built Colonial-style estate that Hernan bought in 2017 was a hot commodity, seeing as Oppenheim had initially hoped to snap up the property for himself, Hernan, 34, reveals to Realtor.com in the latest Celebrity Sanctuary.

“Funny enough, Jason really wanted to buy this house but he had just purchased another home, so he wanted someone that he at least knows to get it. I ended up buying it off market with Jason as my broker,” she explains.

Throughout the house hunt, Oppenheim encouraged Hernan to learn the real estate ropes so she could go from being his client to becoming his coworker and costar. After getting her real estate license in 2018, she “immediately hung [her] license with The O Group … and ended up on the show.”

Though Hernan left “Selling Sunset” in 2025 after six seasons as a main cast member, she still works with Oppenheim and other former costars—just without the added conflict that comes with filming reality TV.

“I would describe it in one word: Peaceful,” Hernan says about her experience in the office now that she’s not on the show.

However, Hernan still credits the series for giving her a platform to pursue other ventures alongside luxury real estate, such as her frozen seafood and empanada brand, Coast to Coast Kitchen, which officially debuted in 2025 but had been in the works for decades.

Hernan “grew up passing out crab cakes at demos and supermarkets” because her grandfather was the founder of the Massachusetts-based seafood company, Yankee Trader Seafood. When Hernan’s mother and aunt took over and needed capital to keep the enterprise going, Hernan lent them money she had earned from modeling, nannying, and investing in the stock market.

Beyond providing funding for equipment and employees, Hernan even bought a manufacturing facility in Hingham, MA that still services her family’s company as well as other food brands. She also owns a house in Norwell, MA next door to her brother’s abode, and is often in the area because of business and her boyfriend.

“Obviously, Boston is very special to me, but L.A.—I created Coast to Coast out of that kitchen with family,” she shares to illustrate why her West Coast residence holds a special place in her heart.

In this edition of Celebrity Sanctuary, Hernan points out the potential she’s always seen in the 3,000-square-foot, four-bedroom, four-bathroom, two-story dwelling she shares with her two dogs and eight rescue cats. Plus, she opens up about how the familiar New England feel of her home kitchen helps her feed every passion.

I purchased the home in 2017 for $2.7 million and … was renting it out. I had it as an investment property because it was a bit big for me by myself. When I started filming the show, my house is super conveniently located to the office, so I moved in right when I started filming.

This specific house and street, it's super conveniently located. It’s in the heart of West Hollywood. The office is right there. The location is a 10 for sure.

I redid the pool. The flooring is original and that's something that I go back and forth with changing, even though I do want to re-do the floors and warm them up. They're wood floors, original from 1940.

I'm definitely gonna do a pretty big remodel. It's very home-y, but it needs updates and I'm super excited to do that. I’m gonna do the full landscaping. It needs new floors, windows, all the things, but I think it'll be a really fun project.

I haven't really made it my own besides the kitchen, which I would say is my sanctuary: somewhere that feels safe, homey, and peaceful. That's really important. My life is very public and having that peace and a place that feels home-y and safe, that's definitely what [sanctuary] means to me.

“Selling Sunset” [was] different than [selling] real estate because [reality TV is] a little bit more drama heavy, so … a lot of times when I would come home from filming, cooking and creating meals for my friends and my family really did help separate that scene that we just had that was so crazy and so hectic. Coming home and forgetting all about that, chopping the vegetables that I was gonna serve for dinner, and really being able to separate the two—I did that all in the kitchen.

The kitchen, when I bought it, was definitely one of my favorite things about the whole house. It reminded me about New England and my family. I added some family photos. I’m from Scituate, MA. I added this cool little Scituate plaque.

It’s bright and white, but there's a lot of wood in there, too, which warms it up. Granite countertops, they're white. It's a very warm and bright kitchen. There's a lot of light that comes through. It really is my favorite part of the whole home.

The dining room area … I have a really beautiful [Restoration Hardware] dining room table that I love. And then I have this little countertop area.

I've created businesses there. I’ve closed deals there. I've had family gatherings there. I’ve had Thanksgiving there, Christmas there, and so many fun little taco nights with my friends that now became my family. I’ve gone on QVC live from the kitchen. I have been in glam for “Selling Sunset.” So many of my interviews—everything's from my kitchen. It’s really special to me.

The stove was literally where I created half of my recipes for Coast to Coast. So many meals are created in there. I love to cook. It's such a passion of mine. It’s therapeutic for me and that's why I was like, “I need to start my own company.

I'm gonna get a new oven, a new SubZero, and all of that. The one thing that it's lacking is storage. I had this open space area where there's glasses, but there's not enough cabinetry, especially for the amount of cooking that I do.

I definitely tend to overcook because I'd rather have more than enough food than not enough. I love to cook and have many options for people. It's funny because my mom and my dad are like, “Do you need help? What do you need help with?” And I really don't need help. I love doing it. I love making every dish, making it special. I love plating it and making it look really good.

Presentation is key. I love it on a white plate, all decorative. I like everything to match. I love it to look nice, even when I'm setting up the table with nice placemats and making the table look really nice.

Some of the stuff is antique. All of my stuff in Boston was my grandmother's that was passed down. Then I've just gotten a lot of the white, classic, Crate and Barrel stuff for the L.A. [kitchen] because I'm not going to ship my really nice stuff over to L.A., especially our sentimental family pieces.

All of my guests, as soon as somebody walks in, I'm like, “What can I make you?” It doesn't matter if they're stopping over for 10 minutes. I have friends that will pop over and I’ll be like, “Do you want me to make you a sandwich? Do you want me to make you a quesadilla or throw in my empanadas?” Making people feel at home makes a difference.

What's really special about the two industries that I'm in that I genuinely love so much—it doesn't feel like work to me. I'm super grateful and I thoroughly enjoy both.

#5502. Hosting Changes How People See Their Home Designs: Survey

Group of friends celebrating at home having dinner

Hosting for the holidays can be chaos—you have to think about decorating, cooking, baking and more. But, there’s another wrench in the planning that people may forget to consider: the setup of your home. Do you have enough space? Enough parking? Enough bathrooms?

A new survey found that more and more homebuyers are taking hosting into consideration when making decisions about the design of their homes.

Homebuilder KB Home’s survey—featuring input from 2,000 U.S. adults and conducted via Talker Research—found that 58% of respondents feel that hosting has made them rethink what they want in their current or future home. While 29% of respondents said that having people over makes them feel proud of their home, 20% report that it makes them feel self-conscious.

“Hosting friends and family can highlight what people love about their homes and what they wish worked better,” said Gena Kirk, vice president of corporate design for KB Home.

As for what people are looking for, the survey reported that 35% said an open living area is the most important feature for making a home comfortable for hosting friends and family during holidays and special occasions, followed by outdoor entertaining space (30%). Other wants include a spacious kitchen (24%), an open kitchen (21%) and a large or dedicated dining area (21%).

Kirk recommended that buyers pursue new homes in order to achieve total customization.

“From spacious living areas and open floor plans to finishes that reflect personal style, a KB home works for everyday life as well as special occasions,” she said. “Our Built-to-Order approach recognizes that no two households are alike, giving buyers the flexibility to make choices that fit their lifestyle and budget and create a home that is uniquely their own.”

Hosting also inspires new priorities, as 21% of respondents said that hosting makes them think about how to make their home more welcoming or comfortable, while 25% said it makes them want to declutter or clean more often. In addition, 24% said that when they host, they notice things about their home they would want to change.

Homebuyers are gaining leverage across much of the country, but assuming every seller is ready to accept a discount could leave them misreading their local market. Read more.

#5498. ‘We Got an Abandoned Mobile Home for Free–and Spent $14K Transforming It’

An Oregon family transformed a mobile home that had sat abandoned for nearly five years into a home for a loved one–all without paying a dime for the property itself.

But getting the home for free was only the beginning. What followed was months of demolition, electrical and plumbing work, drywall installation, and a race to get the aging property ready for its new owner.

Lyman Branson II, who documented the transformation on I Can Fix That, his YouTube channel, took on the ambitious renovation alongside his family with one goal in mind: creating a safe, comfortable home for his sister, Betty Branson, 42, and her 17-year-old twin daughters.

“I don't think I've ever had an opportunity like this before in my life, and so to turn it down would have been a shame,” Betty tells Realtor.com®. “And I know I would have regretted it, so this was probably one of the better decisions I've made in my life.”

The family spent approximately $14,000 transforming the 1977 mobile home—a fraction of what Betty spent on rent in a year. Betty finally moved in the first week of May 2026, and now, just six months later, she is hosting her first Thanksgiving in the home her family helped bring back to life.

Lyman has worked in rental property maintenance and renovation since 2001, so he knew about the home in his small town of Irrigon, OR, that had been abandoned by the owner about five years earlier.

He discussed taking over the mobile home to renovate it and rent it out to someone in need. The landlord would be able to transfer the title to Lyman and later collect rent on the lot. Meanwhile, Lyman would be able to remove the property from the landlord’s possession.

“It was kind of like a ‘I scratch your back, you scratch my back’ kind of deal,” Branson tells Realtor.com.

Initially, Lyman saw the renovation as another project for his YouTube channel, which he launched in early 2025. But the timing was also opportune for his sister, whose living circumstances had unexpectedly changed just days before he called.

Betty had been searching for another rental and considered buying an RV, paying approximately $800 a month for space at an RV park. Instead, her brother presented her with an opportunity to finally own a place of her own.

Betty could contribute what her brother calls “sweat equity,” working on the property before and after her regular job.

The purchase price was zero, but the property was far from move-in ready. The floors and walls were rotted, and there were leaks, water damage, and missing sections of ceiling.

“Basically, it was ready for the dump,” Lyman says.

With more than two decades of experience in the industry, he recognized that the structure was salvageable and the renovation worthwhile. Betty, however, was less convinced.

“I was a little overwhelmed and kind of scared when I first saw it,” she recalls.

She saw the home's many problems, including the broken countertop and the hole in the wall where a window would later be installed.

The home remained in its original location, eliminating the expense of transporting it. However, it was still sitting on flat tires and had never been properly set up. So the family's first task was to stabilize the structure on blocks.

The landlord waived the lot rent for six months while the family obtained the necessary permits. Renovation began in October 2025. Lyman and his father, with help from other family members, updated the almost 50-year-old mobile home to current building codes.

They replaced broken flooring, added insulation and drywall, and wrapped the outside of the home to protect it from the elements. Lyman shared the process on his YouTube channel.

Walls were painted, the bathroom drywall was finished, and the overall interior was beginning to look like a home. But the project wasn't without setbacks.

“There were a couple times that I was still in the middle of it all, and I'm like, 'We're too far in. I can't quit now,'” Betty recalls. “But this is hard and this is scary.”

She had to depend on her brother and her father for help when various issues arose during the renovation.

“I'm so grateful because without them, this wouldn't have been possible for me,”  she says.

Betty received her certificate of occupancy two weeks before the permit expired.

“I was actually really amazed that we were able to make it in the time frame that we did with how much that was done,” she says.

The renovation offered Betty something she had never experienced in 20 years of renting. She got to design the layout of her living space. She got to pick out the locations of her light switches and outlets. Her daughters, who share a bedroom, chose paint colors and the arrangement for the closets.

“It was an experience for me that I'll never forget,” Betty says.

The renovation of the free mobile home came with substantial expenses.

LeAnna Branson, Lyman and Betty's mother, who kept track of the receipts for the renovation, tells Realtor.com that the family initially budgeted between $10,000 and $12,000. However, rising material costs, unexpected damage discovered during demolition, and decisions to upgrade certain features pushed the total to approximately $14,000.

Betty also opted to spend a little more on higher-quality materials and finishes, knowing she intended to live there for years.

“I could have gone cheaper. Definitely, we could have cut some costs here and there,” she says. “But I plan to be here for a while. I want it to last.”

Betty used her savings to kick-start the renovation and lived in her sister’s RV, which allowed her to devote her income to the renovation for six months. Once she moved in and began paying rent on the lot, plus utilities, the pace of the work slowed a bit.

Now, Lyman estimates the renovation is approximately 90% complete. The remaining work involves the upper kitchen cabinets, wall tile, a window replacement, and several finishing touches.

The family also received support from viewers of Lyman's YouTube channel, who contributed an estimated $1,000 to $2,000. Even the handles that will adorn Betty's kitchen cabinets and drawers were paid for by a viewer.

“More support than I ever imagined,” Lyman says of the response to the project. His viewers “loved seeing the family aspect.”

For Betty, the financial benefits extend well beyond the renovation costs. She says she has more living space than she would have gotten in an apartment. And there's space for her daughters and her dog.

“We went over budget a little, but considering [Betty] was paying $20,000 a year to rent, $14,000 is not that bad,” LeAnna says. “I mean it's a chunk of money, but it's doable.”

Lyman believes owning a mobile home, even when you must rent the land it sits on, can offer an affordable housing alternative to people struggling to keep up with rising rental costs across the country.

“That was important for Betty as well, so that she could afford to live the life she deserves,” he says.

Though Betty’s experience shows that acquiring a free or inexpensive mobile home is only a small part of the financial equation, her brother’s professional experience, the family’s help, and the landlord’s willingness to waive her lot rent during the renovation also helped keep costs manageable.

For her parents, seeing their daughter choose everything from her kitchen sink to her bathroom tile was particularly rewarding.

“It gave us a peace of mind to know, you know, that she finally has a place of her own to call her home,” her mother says.

Some of the most special features of her new home are things visitors won’t see. Behind her new cupboards are messages from her family who helped her renovate her home.

“I have places on the wall behind some of the cupboards where the family all, like, signed their names and left me love notes,” Betty says. “I know they're there, even though some of them are covered up.”

The transformation is a daily reminder of what her family made possible.

“The fact that it was my family that assisted me along the way makes it even more special,” she says. “It wasn't just hiring outside help, but family and friends that came to put in the time and effort that they could to help. It makes it mean so much more to me.”

#5497. Anthropic is trying to kill traditional desktop apps with Claude-generated desktop apps

Rarely a day goes by that Anthropic PBC doesn’t announce some kind of new capability, feature or model, and today wasn’t any different. Today came the ability to use Claude to create fully functional desktop applications for Windows and Mac computers with a single prompt.

It promises to be one of its more impactful updates, fanning the flames of those who argue that artificial intelligence is ultimately destined to eat the software world.

The company said today that users can now transform what it calls “artifacts” into standalone applications that run independently of Claude and can be accessed from the desktop. Artifacts have been around for a while, and they can be almost anything, such as a simple order tracker or a meeting dashboard that pulls information from the user’s calendar and email inbox.

However, until today, artifacts were a bit tricky to access. They could be opened up only from inside Claude itself, which meant users first had to open up the chatbot, login and then find the old conversation where they originally created the artifact they want to use.

Anthropic said people are using Claude artifacts all the time for various everyday tasks, and so it makes sense to mature the concept. “If you rely on a tool for work, it should open like the rest of your apps and remind you when something needs your attention,” the company said.

That’s why Anthropic is making it possible for people to use artifacts to create, run and share desktop applications with Claude’s new “Install as App” feature, which is available in beta now on Windows and macOS.

In a video posted on X, Anthropic showed how straightforward it is to create a functional desktop app from a simple prompt. The user simply describes the tool they want Claude to create, click confirm and then sit back and wait for a few seconds as it slaps together the required code to bring that app to life.

You can now install Claude artifacts as desktop apps on Mac and Windows.

Ask Claude to build an artifact, click "Install as app", and open it like any other app. It can use your connectors and, if you allow it, send notifications or add a menu bar item. pic.twitter.com/8CBgqe5OKq

— ClaudeDevs (@ClaudeDevs) November 24, 2026

Because these are “real” apps, they come with their own app icons and they open in a dedicated Window, rather than running within the Claude interface. They also get the ability to send notifications to users, Anthropic said.

As an added benefit, Claude artifacts that are transformed into desktop apps will be able to use Claude and various third-party connectors, meaning that AI agents will be able to interact with them autonomously, Anthropic said. However, the company did warn that any requests made by an app to Claude will count toward their monthly credit usage, which means it could become expensive if an app is used excessively.

In a blog post Anthropic showcased a number of examples of what its internal teams have built, including a fully featured image editing app called Linnet, a file manager with a cinematic design called Phosphor, and a terminal application that integrates with Claude, which is known as Tern.

There is one major caveat to Claude artifacts-as-apps that sets them apart from traditional desktop applications. According to Anthropic, “you need to be online and signed in to Claude to open an app.”

That could be a pretty big downside, for many desktop applications are designed to work even if the computer is not connected to the internet. But those who lack a Wi-Fi connection will be unable to access their Claude-generated apps, even if they’re already built and configured.

#5496. Why the Northeast Could Lead a Factory-Built Housing Boom

Most Americans picture sun-drenched mobile home parks across the South and Southeast when they think of manufactured housing, but more manufactured housing may soon start popping up across the Northeast and West.

A new economic research report from Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner takes an in-depth look at the manufactured housing guidelines in the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which became law in June.

Berner found that cities across the Northeast—including Hartford, CT, Allentown, PA, and Albany, NY—have ideal conditions for a manufactured housing boom: “affordable land, unaffordable traditional new construction, and a low share of single-family starter home inventory.”If you’re not quite sure about what “manufactured housing" means, you’re not alone. For years, people seemingly used “mobile home” and “manufactured housing” interchangeably. But they’re not the same thing.

For one, the “mobile home” classification was retired in 1980, though many still use it colloquially. That year, it was replaced by the term “manufactured home.” Broadly, manufactured homes are those built in a factory and then transported to a site.

For years, federal Housing and Urban Development code required that all manufactured homes have a permanent steel towing frame underneath. New provisions in the Road to Housing Act, meant to spur more affordable housing, eliminated that requirement.

The act further entitles these new chassis-free homes to the same financing, titling, insurance, taxes, transport, and installation as conventional homes.

The hope is that creating this new category of manufactured home will help blunt one of the housing industry’s sharpest pain points: affordable starter homes.

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of affordable starter homes for sale has markedly decreased.

Realtor.com research found roughly 300,000 fewer affordable “starter” listings on the market today than before the pandemic. The cost of those starter homes rose from $256,000 in 2019 to $344,000 in 2026. By comparison, the median price of a manufactured home in April 2026 was $134,800.

To understand what metros might see the biggest impact from this new type of manufactured home, Realtor.com scored the 100 largest metro areas on three metrics: the percentage of single-family starter homes (defined as listings priced at or below 80% of the local median) in the area; the relative price-per-square-foot premiums for traditional new construction; and the availability of affordable vacant land.

Six of the 10 opportunity metros were in the Northeast, including Hartford; Allentown; Albany; Rochester, NY; Syracuse, NY; and Worcester, MA. Other metros that made the list were Denver; Colorado Springs, CO; Albuquerque, NM; and Spokane, WA.

In Hartford, which ranked first, starter homes account for just 17.9% of single-family inventory, while site-built new construction costs 29.1% more per square foot than existing homes.

In third-ranked Allentown, single-family starter homes made up 22.9% of housing in the area, but new-construction costs were 33.6% more than existing homes. In sixth-ranked Albany, starter homes comprised 31.6% of the single-family inventory, but the price per square foot for new construction is 47% higher than for existing homes.

That’s nothing compared with seventh-ranked Rochester, where 33.7% of homes are starter but site-built new construction costs 97% more per square foot than existing homes.

While the economics in these cities are compelling, another reason manufactured housing may become more popular in these metros is that frigid Northeastern winters limit conventional housing construction. Meanwhile, manufactured housing can be assembled year-round.

Before Hartford, Albany, or any other metro can begin taking advantage of the Road to Housing Act’s new manufactured housing rules, municipal zoning laws will need to change, Berner found.

According to Land Use Labs data cited in the report, only about 17% of zoned land nationwide explicitly permits manufactured housing communities, and many municipalities enforce minimum floor-size rules or design restrictions that block factory-built units.

#5495. Regional Spotlight: California Home Sales Hit Lowest Level as Prices, Mortgage Rates Rise

(TNS)–As the year comes to an end, California’s housing market has slowed down.

Existing home sales have dropped to their lowest level in nearly three years as high mortgage rates and affordability challenges continue.

“Homebuying activity weakened across California in October, pushing sales to their lowest level in nearly three years as elevated mortgage rates and low affordability remained significant hurdles for prospective buyers,” the California Association of Realtors said in its latest housing report, released on Tuesday, Nov. 17.

Existing single-family home sales totaled 246,830 in October.

That is a decrease of 5.2% from the 260,410 sales in September and 12.7% from the 282,760 sales in October 2025.

“When mortgage rates jumped to a nearly three-year high in late September, we saw many buyers step back and reassess what they could afford, which led to fewer closed sales in October,” California Association of Realtors President Mark Peterson said in the report.

Despite the slowdown in sales, real estate experts said, home prices remained relatively steady, while mortgage rates continued to pose a challenge for potential buyers.

What can California homebuyers expect to pay?

Here’s what to know about home prices, mortgage rates and where buyers can find more affordable options across the state:

How much does buying a home cost in California?

The statewide median home price was $886,760 in October, according to the California Association of Realtors.

That was down 1.4% from $899,720 in September but barely changed from $887,330 in October 2025.

California’s median home price previously reached a record $930,260 in May.

“Home prices held steady, suggesting that buyers are still engaged and sellers remain confident in the value of their homes despite the near-term slowdown,” Peterson said.

Still, affordability remains a major obstacle for many prospective homebuyers across the state.

How much are current mortgage rates in California?

Mortgage rates continued to climb in October, adding to the challenges facing homebuyers, according to the California Association of Realtors.

The group’s report put the average mortgage rate at 7.33%—up from the 6.86% in September and 6.25% in October 2025.

Zillow listed the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in California at about 7.38%, as of Thursday, Nov. 19.

The combination of higher borrowing costs and economic uncertainty could continue to weigh on home sales in the coming year, according to Jordan Levine, the California Association of Realtors’ senior vice president and chief economist.

“The housing market is facing renewed headwinds as inflation remains elevated and the stock market loses momentum,” Levine said in the housing report. “Home sales will likely remain soft in the near term, but pent-up demand continues to build as many prospective buyers stay on the sidelines.”

If geopolitical tensions and economic uncertainty ease, Levine said, California “should see more of those buyers gradually return to the market.”

Where can I find homes under $400,000 in California?

Despite California housing some of the most expensive home prices in the country, some counties still have median home prices below the statewide median of $886,760.

According to the California Association of Realtors, the state’s most affordable homes can be found in Northern California, with a median price of $385,000.

“The relationship to the earth and forest shifts from very grounded on the landward side of the house to a more perched position at the water side. The main living volume rises above the adjacent wings, allowing clerestory windows on three sides to bring filtered natural light deep into the interior. Generous openings on the north and south sides promote passive ventilation, eliminating the need for air conditioning.

#5493. Attached Homes Drive Salt Lake City’s New-Home Sales Growth

New home demand in Salt Lake City is increasingly splitting along product lines, with attached housing gaining momentum while detached sales remain comparatively flat.

In September, annualized new-home sales across the metro topped 2,800 units, up roughly 4% from a year ago. Attached housing drove much of the gain, with annualized sales reaching 1,350 units, a 10% increase year over year. Meanwhile, detached sales remained slightly higher at 1,450 units but edged down 0.7% from last year.

Although detached homes still accounted for more sales in absolute terms, virtually all of the market’s recent growth stemmed from attached product. Active project counts showed a similar pattern. As of November, Salt Lake City had 92 active detached new-home projects, down 3.2%, compared with 65 attached projects, up 3.2%.

Pricing helps explain why attached housing may be resonating with buyers, especially given today’s affordability challenges. As of July, the average list price for a new detached home was roughly $738,000, up 11% from a year earlier, while new attached homes averaged approximately $470,000, up about 4%. That puts the difference between the two averages at more than $268,000, although it is important to note that attached and detached homes differ in size, location, design, and community mix.

The distribution of closings reinforces that distinction. In the past 12 months ending August, attached new-home closings were concentrated heavily in lower price bands, particularly between $350,000 and $450,000. Detached closings were distributed much more broadly, with the most substantial shares falling between $450,000 and $650,000.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth market reports published in Zonda Enterprise.

During this year’s Bike to Cure weekend, 170 Oatey associates from locations around the world came together to ride, volunteer, and raise funds for cancer research at Cleveland Clinic.

Close to three decades ago, Hearthstone and BUILDER joined forces to create an annual award that recognizes home builders who are dedicated to giving back and making a difference in their communities. For upcoming 2027, the Hearthstone BUILDER Humanitarian Award will honor its 28th inductee.

The 2027 winner will be recognized during an in-person awards ceremony at the Builder 100 Leadership Summit, taking place May 3 to 5 in Dana Point, California.

2026: Allan Merrill of Beazer Homes earned the Hearthstone honor in 2026. What began with a single race by Merrill has since expanded into a company-wide model of giving, anchored by a national nonprofit partnership with the Fisher House Foundation, sustained funding, and employee participation and pride.

2025: The Lennar Foundation, the charitable arm of Lennar Corp., was awarded in 2025. Created in 1989 to give back to the communities in which Lennar builds, the foundation has focused on many causes including helping veterans transition to civilian life, offering job training to formerly incarcerated individuals, funding life-saving medical research, and more.

2024: Pat Neal was recognized in 2024 for his dedication to land preservation in his home state of Florida. During his development career, the founder and chairman of Neal Communities has balanced developing land for homes and preserving it for future generations.

2023: Recognized as a collective company, Meritage Homes has supported countless charitable causes in its 40-year history. 2022: As a fourth-generation home builder, HistoryMaker Homes CEO Nelson Mitchell has a servant heart that has been passed down through generations. 2021: Taylor Morrison’s chairman and CEO Sheryl Palmer fosters a workplace that continually gives back. 2021: Edward Burr, the CEO of GreenPointe Holdings, started the Monique Burr Foundation for Children, an after-school program designed to educate and empower children against abuse, bullying and victimization, in honor of his late wife. #5489. Eight Guidelines for Brokerage Growth

Above from left to right: Jackie Louh, Rob Cleapor, John Finn and Doug Smith, on stage at RISMedia’s 38th Annual CEO & Leadership Exchange in Washington, D.C. this past October. Not pictured, Amy Somerville.

Business owners are constantly on the look-out for the best ways to evolve and grow their firms, and real estate broker/owners are no different. However, in today’s unpredictable market environment, growth can be an elusive goal, and taking a brokerage to the next level requires clarity, commitment and creativity.

A group of brokerage leaders addressed the growth dilemma at RISMedia’s 2026 CEO & Leadership Exchange this past fall during the panel discussion “More Than One Way to Grow.” Here’s their top advice for achieving growth despite current challenges that can feel insurmountable.

1. Take a broad approach. According to Jackie Louh, chief operating officer of Lamacchia Realty, increasing business means diversifying your efforts to ensure you’re growing on a variety of fronts, such as: expanding the brokerage footprint, increasing agent productivity, increasing market share and growing agent count.

“To do that, we have different people focused on those different avenues,” said Louh “Anthony (Lamacchia, company CEO) and I, for instance, we focus primarily on what we call chunk growth—acquisition opportunities. And then we have our regional sales managers who are focused every day on organic growth. They work with recruiting in their markets. They work with helping the agents in their markets grow their business. It’s not just about being the biggest company. We want to be the best, and to do that and to grow, you have to hit all avenues of that growth.”

2. Support agents and franchisees. Rob Cleapor, CEO of the growing franchise Iron Valley Real Estate, admitted that early on, growth equated to agent count. He soon realized, however, that the number of agents was not as important as the quality of those agents.

“As we started growing rapidly, you start realizing that’s really not what’s important,” said Cleapor. “For us, the way we define growth is supporting our agents and our franchisees along the way. “Growth, like (Jackie) said, is agent count, it’s footprint. But more importantly for me, it’s the support that you give for franchisees and the agents, and making sure that we’re keeping that support at the top so that everybody can grow and grow the right way.”

Echoing Cleapor’s sentiments, Doug Smith, founder and CEO of Douglas Realty is zeroing in on productivity.

“Our growth this year from an agent headcount is about 12%,” he said. “Our transactions are up almost 45% in this crazy down market. So we focus a ton on training, a ton on bringing in good agents.”

3. Talk to teams…and tired brokers. As John Finn, CEO and senior managing broker of United Real Estate Richmond pointed out, the majority of brokerages in his market—and across the country—are small, many with 10 agents or less. That’s why his growth strategy has focused on bringing successful teams into the fold.

“We have people who had good teams and decided they wanted to be brokers, and then woke up one day and said, ‘Oh, I really don’t want to do this.’ We have had great success with that,” said Finn.

Finn also homes in on brokers that want to go back to being agents.

“We’ve had success with older agents who really want to get back to the business of actually selling real estate and not having to provide the back-office services, the payroll, the tech stack, AI…things they don’t want to deal with anymore,” he said.

4. Build the right infrastructure. As panel moderator Amy Somerville, COO of the Real REMAX Group noted, the definition of brokerage growth changes when you put the word “sustainable” in front of it.

“I want to talk about the internal infrastructure and what needs to be set up to support the growth that you plan for your business,” she said. “Technology systems, financial systems, general infrastructure.”

Finn discussed the benefit of tapping into the tech stack of a large parent company like United.

“I found that by the time I studied and researched state-of-the-art (technology) and developed state of the art and got the money together to buy state of the art and got the agents to use state of the art, it wouldn’t be state of the art anymore,” he explained. “When we’re out approaching other people about coming to join our team, I don’t have to worry about AI as many other smaller firms in my market do, because I’ve got United in my pocket.”

5. Work on your business, not in it. In the early days of Iron Valley, Cleapor quickly learned that sustainable growth meant putting the right team in place, then delegating accordingly.

“Early on, I was managing three offices. I was the director of marketing. I did all of our graphic design. I did our franchise sales,” he shared. “One of my favorite lines somebody said to me years ago was, ‘When you’re doing 10 things, 10 things are getting 10% of your effort. And when you only do one thing, it gets 100% of your effort.’ Putting the infrastructure in, the processes, and more importantly, the people on your team…you have to make that decision or everything that you’ve grown is going to collapse.”

6. Set acquisition criteria and stick to it. Growing a real estate brokerage by acquiring another brokerage can quickly expand a firm’s business—provided a specific strategy is in place and adhered to.

Louh, for example, says that focusing on firms located in contiguous states is usually the best path. She then targets legacy firms within those states.

“The (firms) that have been around a long time have really built a strong brand and they have agents that have been with them a long time,” she said. “That makes for a much smoother transition because the agents trust the owner. They’re going to do whatever the owner says. They’re going to go wherever the owner goes.”

When considering a firm to acquire, Louh also advised making sure the owner is focused on their agents, not themselves.

“If the owner is saying, ‘How is this going to benefit me? How much money am I going to make off of this?’ that is not a company we want to align with,” she said. “If the owner isn’t invested in their agents, if that acquisition does come together, the owner’s going to basically disappear. They’re going to collect their paycheck. They’re not going to work to retain the agents. They’re not going to work to recruit, and then we’re just going to end up losing those agents.”

7. Always be networking. Smith reminded everyone that real estate is a people business, and staying committed to building relationships with other brokers can lead to organic M&A opportunities when values align.

“Last year we acquired a 50-agent brokerage, and it kind of happened by accident,” he said. “The owner of that brokerage was president of our local Realtor board and he invited me to speak. We didn’t know each other, but it turns out we were very much in alignment on so many different things in business. And it just so happened that his franchise renewal was up and he pulled me to the side and said, ‘Hey, we should talk.’ So it started there.”

8. Grow horizontally. While firms traditionally want to grow vertically—more agents, more transactions—in the current market, brokerages need to take a closer look at growing horizontally by getting more out of the transaction through services such as title, escrow, mortgage, insurance and more.

“The customer is looking for an experience at one stop where they can get everything,” said Finn. “We as agents, we as brokers are going to have to start providing that for our people.”

“The future of our industry is you have to be involved in more than just one area of the transaction or else I think you will get shut out,” agreed Smith. “I think you have to have your hands in a little bit of everything. Provide a consumer experience, create that client for life, but even more and just as important, create that agent for life.”

Maria Patterson is RISMedia’s executive vice president.

#5488. Zoom’s conversations-to-completion strategy is starting to pay off

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Zoom Communications Inc. has spent the better part of the past few years building products to become more than just the video company everyone used during the pandemic. Its fiscal third-quarter results, posted Monday, showed the strategy is working, though more work remains.

Total revenue grew 4.9%, but enterprise revenue rose 8.6%, its fastest pace in 13 quarters. Zoom raised its full-year outlook and announced its first quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share.

The acceleration should be viewed not as a one-quarter anomaly but as a manifestation of the strategy the company outlined at Zoomtopia about a month ago – moving from “conversations to completion.” That strategy gives customers a reason to buy more of Zoom and builds a competitive moat wider than most investors realize.

The concept of conversations to completion has enough merit that Microsoft used those exact words at its recent Ignite 2026 event. In fact, it held an entire session on the topic. Though having an 800-pound gorilla like Microsoft jump on a trend might seem threatening, Zoom has a significant lead and can use Microsoft’s marketing to add momentum to its current tailwind.

Nearly all work starts with a conversation: a meeting, a call, a chat thread or a customer interaction. Then everyone leaves, and the real work begins: updating the customer record, writing the follow-up and scheduling the next step. Collaboration vendors have always owned the first step, leaving the second to someone else.

Zoom wants both. “We’d like to leverage AI to transform our business from a conversation-centric vendor to a system of completions,” Chief Executive Eric Yuan said on the earnings call. He later put it more plainly: “Conversation is step 1. Step 2, AI will take over.”

His proof point was Zoom’s own sales organization, which uses ZoomMate, the company’s agentic framework. Sellers, Yuan said, “no longer log into the backend CRM system.” The agent takes over after the call ends. In enterprise software, value is shifting from where work is recorded to where it originates.

AI agents are quickly becoming a commodity, and so are the models behind them. What is scarce is context, the knowledge of what was decided, by whom, and why. Zoom sits on the richest source of it in most companies: what people actually said to one another and to customers.

“Any agent without context really cannot get work done,” Yuan said. That’s why the unified context layer Zoom showcased at Zoomtopia is central to the story. It links conversations to chats, documents and third-party systems, ensuring people and agents work from the same information.

My Notes, the company’s AI note-taker, extends that reach to third-party and in-person conversations. Yuan said it is nearing 2 million monthly active users, with one financial services firm rolling it out to 80,000 wealth advisers. Chief Financial Officer Michelle Chang added that online customers using My Notes have been associated with a 50% reduction in churn.

That is what will create a deeper competitive moat for Zoom. The more context a customer stores with Zoom, the more useful its agents become and the harder it is to leave. Zoom’s moat is not the meeting. Think of it as the memory of the meeting.

A context layer is only as good as the number of conversations it ingests, and this is where Zoom’s breadth of platforms matters. Meetings, phone, chat, contact center and now sales intelligence all feed into the same foundation, and each product gets smarter from the others.

Customers are consolidating. DSI Systems is replacing five separate products with Zoom. SolarWinds expanded its Zoom licenses while “recalibrating its Microsoft package,” according to Yuan. Enterprise net dollar expansion returned to 100%, its highest level in 11 quarters. “Strong RPO growth reflects our continued success in landing larger, longer-term multiproduct platform deals, demonstrating growing demand for our AI-first platform,” Chang said.

Customer experience is where completion gets paid for. Zoom CX recurring revenue grew in the high double digits for the seventh straight quarter, and all 10 of its largest CX deals included paid AI. More telling, Zoom said at Zoomtopia that 90% of its top 100 CX deals in the first half were with customers new to Zoom. Contact center is no longer a cross-sell. It is a front door.

Chang described the differentiation as “the ability to think about customer experience in a whole and fresh new way.” Specifically, she said, “to be able to seamlessly hand off from virtual agents to agents assisted with AI is a big winner for us.” AI-native startups have the virtual agent but not the human side. Legacy contact center vendors have the humans but not the pace of innovation. Zoom has both on one platform.

There is also an economic moat. Zoom runs most of its AI workload on its own small models and saves the expensive frontier models for harder tasks. “I fundamentally believe no single model can satisfy everything,” Yuan said. Gross margin rose even as AI usage grew, a feat that a point product reselling another company’s tokens cannot easily match.

The quarter was strong, but analyst questions revealed several concerns.

Some will read the dividend as a sign of maturity. With more than $7 billion in cash and free cash flow margins above 40%, I see a company that can fund innovation and return capital at the same time.

Although these issues came up during the call, most of the investment community remains positive about Zoom. In his note, Arun Bhatia of William Blair wrote, “Churn and downsell rates are becoming more favorable, AI usage and monetization are increasing, and adoption of new products such as Phone and Zoom CX is strong. We are encouraged by these trends and see potential for a growth uptick in the future.”

Zoom’s headline growth resembles that of a mature software vendor, but the company is in transition, so it’s important to look beyond the numbers. The underlying enterprise business is built to be a platform that uses context to drive customers toward more products and longer commitments. Investors should watch enterprise growth, net expansion and CX AI attach rates rather than the top line.

For information technology and business leaders, the lesson extends beyond Zoom. Conversation data is a strategic asset, so decide deliberately where it lives and which agents can act on it. Insist on openness so that context can feed the tools you choose. Start where completion is easy to measure, in the contact center and in sales.

That is where Zoom is proving that the conversation was never the product. The outcome is.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

At the end of a private drive in Park City, UT, a mountain modern home with views of not one but two ski resorts has come on the market for $15,250,000.

Designed by Aspen-based CCY Architects, the home at 15 Eagle Pointe Court balances modernist sophistication with mountain coziness, featuring Telluride Gold stonework, an oxidized Corten steel roof and Western red cedar siding.

"Modern lines of steel and glass are paired with warm wood finishes and natural stone, providing seamless indoor-outdoor living within a private mountain landscape," says listing agent Michael LaPay of Summit Sotheby's International Realty Park City.

LaPay knows the house well. He represented the original owners, who built it in 2005, and has handled its last two sales as well.

The four-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom residence spans 7,053 square feet on 2.69 acres in Park Meadows.

"This property's size and location at the end of a private drive is a rarity in the coveted Park Meadows neighborhood, positioned on a height of land that takes in panoramic ski run views," LaPay says.

Inside, the floors are French Vanilla slate from India. The great room opens to a south-facing deck that looks out at the runs of Park City Mountain Resort and Deer Valley Resort, each 10 to 15 minutes away.

Recent renovations reworked the kitchen and bathrooms. The kitchen now has gourmet appliances, custom cabinetry and an oversized island topped in marble, and the primary bathroom comes with an expansive steam shower. Other updates include a custom bunkroom, a gym and outdoor turf areas for recreation.

Outside, heated patios are linked by sculptural staircases, and the driveway is heated, too. A three-car garage completes the property.

"There is a wonderful walking path up to a summit that is perfect for a 'sundowner' gathering to enjoy sunsets," LaPay says.

The property borders Round Valley, a preserved open space with trails for hiking, biking and cross-country skiing that are maintained year-round.

Besides being close to the area's top ski resorts, the estate is less than 20 minutes from the historic Main Street and its shops, galleries and restaurants, and a five-minute drive from the Park Meadows Country Club.

Salt Lake City International Airport and private terminals in Salt Lake City and Heber City are all about 30 minutes away, close enough for a weekend of skiing.

#5482. Formal verification startup Sequent raises $2.2M to prove code obeys its safety rules

Formal verification startup Sequent Inc. today announced that it has raised $2.2 million in new funding to take its Alan proof platform out of early access.

Founded in London in January, Sequent offers a platform that uses artificial intelligence to find mathematical proofs that code obeys the safety rules its engineers set. Decentralized exchange Curve Finance is its first paying customer.

Curve also figures in how Sequent got started. Chief Executive Charles Cooper, who leads development of Vyper, one of the two main programming languages for Ethereum, inadvertently introduced a flaw into the Vyper compiler in 2021. Though the bug was fixed within months, programs already running on the blockchain could not be updated, leaving older Curve pools and other projects exposed when attackers used the flaw to take more than $50 million in July 2023.

Following the incident, Ramana Kumar, now Sequent’s chief technology officer and formerly an AI safety researcher at Google DeepMind, offered to help prove the Vyper compiler correct. Kumar co-created CakeML, a compiler proved correct all the way down to the instructions a computer runs.

Cooper believes the lesson reaches far beyond crypto, saying that “smart contracts taught us that anything that can be exploited will be.” Banks, governments and companies running older systems have relied on keeping their code private, according to Cooper, who said AI-powered cyberattacks are now eroding that protection.

Alan works today on Vyper smart contracts, with support for Solidity and Solana in development and general software in Rust, C, TypeScript and Python to follow.

For now, engineers using Alan write rules for their code such as “no user can withdraw more than their balance” in plain language, and the job of finding a mathematical proof is handed to AI. Nothing the AI comes up with is taken on trust, as each proof has to get through HOL4, a checker Kumar has helped build for more than a decade.

For two-coin StableSwap pools holding standard tokens, Alan was used to prove that no user can take more than a set limit from depositors, whatever they do and in whatever order. The work also found minor accounting and rounding errors, none of which breached the limit. The founders are now proving the Vyper compiler itself, since the Curve proof does not cover the compiler where the 2021 flaw sat.

Along with AI computing costs, the funding will pay for engineering, sales and marketing hires. Subscriptions to Alan start at $99 a month for individuals, with auditor plans priced at $200 a month and team plans starting at $500 a month.

Frachtis and Metaplanet Holdings OÜ co-led the pre-seed round. Metaplanet is the investment firm of Skype co-founder Jaan Tallinn, who led Anthropic PBC’s Series A round in 2021. According to Frachtis founder Xavier Meegan, crypto is the right place to start, with “billions already at risk.”

#5481. Small Business Owners Reluctant to Take Next Step in Home-Buying Journey: Report

Buying a home is a daunting task for most people, even without considering the latest mortgage rates averaging above 7%.

But how consumers earn an income can greatly affect their transition from homebuyer to homeowner.

A recent survey conducted by mortgage lender Newrez found that small business owners are reluctant to take the next step in their home-buying journeys, while loan officers say that small business owners can qualify for a home much sooner than they realize.

The report found that 77% of mortgage lenders identified tax write-offs/deductions reducing their client’s qualifying income as one of the biggest challenges their small business owner clients face when trying to obtain a mortgage.

“If you’re self-employed, trying to determine if you’ll be eligible for a mortgage isn’t always as simple as asking, ‘How much does my business make?’” the report states. “How your income is documented, the loan program you’re considering and other qualification requirements can all affect your eligibility.”

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Inflation—exacerbated by rising energy costs—has left little breathing room for the average consumer. The latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the Bureau of Labor Statistics found that the all-items index grew 0.4%, a slight decrease from the previous report, but still a “hotter than expected” estimate.

The CPI report attributed the jump to the increases in shelter inflation (up 0.3%), which contributed to over 30% of the increase. Core inflation also grew 0.3% in October, and has been growing at a constant rate for the past few months.

Other challenges that mortgage lenders highlighted include documentation or requirement-related factors. But having an inconsistent/variable income on a monthly basis can make it difficult to lock in a reasonable monthly mortgage payment.

Businesses of any size can feel the squeeze of high prices and operating costs. As of late, homebuilders point to rising labor costs and ongoing inflation pressures as significant challenges, with National Association of Home Builders Chief Economist Robert Dietz highlighting the effect of tariffs on building material costs.

Another aspect the survey dives into is the information available to small business owners. According to the report, 84% of mortgage originators stated that small business owners could qualify for a mortgage sooner than they realize.

“Originators who work with small business owners said awareness is as big a hurdle as financial qualifications,” the report continues. “Sixty-five percent said the two were equally significant, and 75% said lack of awareness was at least as significant, if not more so.”

In the same vein, 71% of mortgage lenders agreed that small business owners tended to be more anxious about the mortgage process than their W-2 counterparts. A significant majority (73%) of mortgage lenders also agree that small business owners assume they won’t qualify for a mortgage, even before speaking with a broker or lender.

“Small business owners have income that isn’t always fully captured by traditional documentation,” Bob Johnson, Newrez head of origination, stated. “Giving our broker partners and loan officers a variety of ways to meet borrowers’ needs helps us make home happen for more small business owners across the country.”

Rising operating costs are not the only issue small business owners face. The New York Times reported that Etsy—an online marketplace geared toward independent creators who sell handmade items and custom products—is facing a significant amount of backlash over a new policy change.

The policy in question reserves Etsy—and its third-party vendors—the right to use sellers’ content to develop and train AI models. Following the company’s new terms, many independent sellers withdrew from the platform, citing anger and dissatisfaction with the company’s turn toward AI, with one creator saying he won’t let his content “be stolen.”

Rather, the platform states that it is using AI actions such as “translating your listing descriptions so buyers around the world can discover your items, or featuring your listing photos in Etsy marketing campaigns to showcase your creative work.”

It’s unclear whether small business owners will flock back to Etsy’s platform, but the situation does shed light on hurdles small businesses may face.

“Mortgage lenders and originators can play an important role in helping these borrowers understand the available options and feel confident navigating the homebuying process,” Johnson added. “Building a business of your own should help you buy a home, not stand in your way.”

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.

#5480. Just 3 Major U.S. Metros Are Seller’s Markets–the Fewest Since the Pandemic Freeze

Just three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas were seller’s markets in October. That’s tied for the fewest in records dating back to 2016, matching April 2020, when the pandemic froze the housing market.

Nassau County, NY was the number-one seller’s market, with 24.7% fewer sellers than buyers. The other seller’s markets were Newark, NJ (-14.3%) and Montgomery County, PA (-12.1%).

All three seller’s markets became less strong seller’s markets in October. In Nassau County, there were 28.3% fewer sellers than buyers in September, a bigger gap than October’s 24.7%. Newark’s gap shrunk from 17.6% to 14.3%, and Montgomery County’s shrunk from 20.1% to 12.1%. Milwaukee, which was a seller’s market in September, is now balanced, meaning it doesn’t favor sellers or buyers.

The seller’s markets are places where limited homebuilding has kept housing supply tight. In the greater New York City area, combine that with strong demand for homes near a major job center, and buyers are competing for homes. Home-sale prices rose an average of 3.3% year over year across the three seller’s markets in October. That’s compared with a 0.3% uptick across all of the buyer’s markets, a sign that in seller’s markets, competition among buyers is pushing up home prices.

“Buyers looking in these pockets of the Northeast should be prepared for a very different experience than buyers elsewhere in the country,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “They may have less room to negotiate, especially on desirable, move-in-ready homes, and could face multiple-offer situations. If you’re shopping in one of these markets, it’s especially important to know your budget, be ready to act when the right home comes along and avoid getting swept up in a bidding war.”

Seller’s markets are the exception to a national picture that heavily favors buyers.

Nationwide, homebuyers have more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records. There were an estimated 70.5% more home sellers than buyers in the U.S. housing market in October, the biggest gap in records dating back to 2013.

That marks the sixth record-breaking month in a row, and the margin is up from 65.6% in September. The Sun Belt is driving the extreme buyer’s market nationwide, led by huge seller surpluses in Miami, Nashville, TN and Las Vegas.

When sellers outnumber buyers, buyers typically have more negotiating power because they have options. That’s why a market with a lot more sellers than buyers is considered a buyer’s market. We define a market where there are over 10% more sellers than buyers as a buyer’s market and a market where there are over 10% fewer sellers than buyers as a seller’s market. A market where the gap is plus or minus 10% is considered a balanced market.

We estimated the number of buyers using proprietary Redfin data on the typical time from a buyer’s first tour to close of purchase, and MLS data on active listings and pending sales. The estimated number of sellers in the market is simply the number of active listings in the MLS. These estimates are seasonally adjusted and subject to revision. See a more detailed methodology here and view an interactive dashboard here.

It’s only a buyer’s market for people who can afford to buy. High housing costs and economic jitters have pushed many would-be homebuyers to back off in recent years, creating the imbalance between buyers and sellers we see today.

“A buyer-friendly market can help make homeownership a little more attainable, even if it doesn’t solve the affordability challenges that have kept many people on the sidelines,” Khan said. “Sellers are increasingly competing for buyers’ attention, which can translate into price reductions, concessions and other savings. First-time buyers don’t have equity from a previous home to put toward a purchase, which makes saving for a down payment a big hurdle–but they also don’t have to sell a home before they can buy or give up a low mortgage rate.  With a historic buyer’s market and home prices that are finally ticking down after three years of increases, first-time buyers who have been waiting–and can afford today’s costs–may have an opportunity to make a move.”

The gap between buyers and sellers widened in October because would-be buyers retreated, while sellers continued listing their homes, albeit at a sluggish pace.

There were an estimated 895,752 homebuyers in the market nationwide in October, the lowest level in records dating back to 2013. That’s down 2% from a month earlier, the sixth straight monthly decline. Mortgage rates averaged 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September, which priced out more would-be buyers.

On the flip side, there were an estimated 1,526,984 home sellers in the market, the most since March 2020. That’s up 0.9% month over month.

The number of homes on the market is piling up because many homes are lingering on the market for months without going under contract. Each month, more new listings are adding to the big pool of supply.

Some homeowners keep listing their houses despite falling demand because many have given up on waiting for lower rates. They may want to sell now because they’re worried prices could decline, and some need to move for a new job, a growing family, or another life change. But many homeowners who don’t need to move have substantial equity and little pressure to sell, so they may hold off on listing.

Over 80% of U.S. metro areas, 41 of the 50 Redfin analyzed, are buyer’s markets. That matches September’s record.

For the third month in a row, Miami and Nashville have the biggest surpluses of sellers over buyers. Miami had 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, and Nashville had 159.5% more. Las Vegas (149.9%) was third on the list. In the top 13 buyer’s markets, there were more than twice as many sellers as buyers in October. Nearly all are in the Sun Belt; four are in Texas and four are in Florida.

The Sun Belt, particularly Texas and Florida, is home to some of the nation’s biggest buyer’s markets, partly because of robust homebuilding. Builders are continuing to add new homes even as demand cools, swelling inventory and giving buyers more options and negotiating power.

Demand has cooled largely because rising mortgage rates and stubbornly high home prices are pricing buyers out. In Florida, rising HOA and homeowners insurance costs are exacerbating the affordability squeeze.

Six metros were “balanced” in October, neither buyer’s nor seller’s markets: Chicago (8.1% more sellers than buyers), Boston (7.5%), Providence, RI (7.5%), New Brunswick, NJ (5.6%), Milwaukee (0.6% fewer sellers than buyers) and San Francisco (6.9% fewer).

The surplus of home sellers over buyers grew month over month in 34 of the 41 buyer’s markets in October.

The surplus increased most in Miami, which also has the biggest surplus of sellers over buyers; there were 195.8% more sellers than buyers in October, up from 160.5% the month before. The next-biggest monthly increases were in Las Vegas, where there were 149.9% more sellers than buyers, up from 122.8%, and Nashville (159.5%, up from 134.3%).

House hunters lost negotiating power in seven buyer’s markets. The surplus of sellers over buyers fell from September to October in Fort Worth, TX (91.6%, down from 100%), St. Louis (23.1%, down from 27.1%), Austin (124.8%, down from 128.2%), Dallas (118.6%, down from 120.5%), Jacksonville, FL, Pittsburgh and Los Angeles. All of them remain buyer’s markets.

As a data journalist at Redfin, Dana Anderson writes about the numbers behind real estate trends.
