#5466. Why This Winter Could Be a Hidden Opportunity for Homebuyers—Plus a New Rate Discount From Chase

The housing market remains tough this winter—but prepared buyers will be presented with opportunities.

"Preparation is everything," says Erik Schmitt, head of consumer direct sales at Chase Home Lending, which is part of JPMorgan Chase's commercial bank.

The outlook for 2027 appears tough. The latest Realtor.com® quarterly construction insights report shows that prices on new homes are holding steady, but builders are having to get creative to attract buyers. Many have said they expect difficulty for much of next year.

On top of that, leaders at the Federal Reserve have signaled that they're poised to raise interest rates multiple times in the next few months to tame inflation. Homeowners are also managing rising insurance costs, HOA fees, and utilities.

Do anything you can now to improve your credit, pay down debt, and understand your budget and what you can afford will help, says Schmitt.

"Get pre-approval because you never know when the market will turn," he advises.

Improving credit scores and paying off higher interest-rate debt will give you more purchasing power.

This week, the National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index plunged to a 14-year low. Meanwhile, the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index showed home values fell for the 16th straight month.

So, in the coming winter there's no question about seasonal weakness in the housing market. In some markets, that means more negotiating power and possibly some better options for buyers. But shrinking inventory might also mean there are fewer options.

For that reason, Schmitt says it's best to be proactive this winter.

"It's difficult to time the rate environment," says Schmitt. "What we advise customers to do is have a strong understanding of what they can afford and what they feel comfortable with. It's difficult to time the market, so if you get in a home that meets your needs, meets your affordability target, in the event rates do rally or reduce, you can always refinance."

From Nov. 30  to Dec. 13, Chase is running a mortgage rate sale of up to 0.25% off for qualified buyers. Both new and existing customers will be able to lock in a lower rate on a new home purchase or refinance loan.

The rate sale discount can be stacked with all existing available Chase Home Lending discounts and programs like its Chase Homebuyer Grant and Relationship Pricing Program.

The stacked savings are still subject to the same terms and conditions, and other programs must have structure that means maximum discounts and limitations.

The bank determined a lot of good buyers remain on the sidelines.

JPMorgan Chase announced earlier this year it would invest $750 billion into the housing market. Its American Dream Initiative aims to build or preserve 1 million affordable housing units and help a half-million customers purchase homes—including 200,000 first-time homebuyers.

"Our focus is where we can help with affordability," says Schmitt.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5465. From Honky-Tonks to High-End Estates: Inside Nashville’s Lasting Luxury Boom

Many metros gave up most or even all of their COVID-19 pandemic-era housing market gains, but some kept on trucking, including Nashville, TN.

"Nashville is one of the pandemic boomtowns that kept its boom," writes Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith in his Nashville Luxury Market Highlight report.

Nashville held on to more of its pandemic run-up than any other major Tennessee metro as of September 2026, says the report.

While the area has been hot for years, demand for its luxury homes accelerated sharply after the pandemic, resulting in a 100% increase in prices from February 2020 to October 2026. Unlike other metros that gave up most or even all of its pandemic-era gains, Nashville has retained a healthy 83.3% of them.

During the pandemic, remote work allowed many people to relocate to Music City, where they could enjoy not only the conveniences and excitement of city life, but also lower prices than wherever they were coming from.

And unlike other midsized metros that saw massive pandemic-era gains—such as Denver and Austin, TX—Nashville's prices have kept afloat. Denver, on the other hand, sits 33% below its pandemic peak, and Austin is 29% below.

Nashville's entry-luxury threshold (the top 10% of listings) now stands at $1.65 million versus $899,000 at the start of the pandemic in February 2020. This is only 8.4% below its peak of $1.80 million in April 2022.

In terms of retention, the only Tennessee city that comes out slightly ahead of Nashville is Knoxville, which pulled ahead in October with a 86.4% retention rate from its pandemic-era highs. But Nashville had to hold on to steeper gains, because its run-up was twice as large as Knoxville's.

Knoxville's entry-luxury threshold currently stands at $1.05 million, a smidge below its peak median price of $1.10 million in May 2023.

Another standout in the state is Chattanooga, which has retained nearly 64% of its pandemic gains, while Cleveland, TN, which had the highest run-up of any metro in the state with 137%, has given up all but 28.6% of that.

Nashville's share of luxury listings has also continued to rise, with million-dollar-plus homes making up 18.9% of its listings in September 2026, up from a mere 8.3% five years ago.

This is 4.6 times more luxe listings than in 2020 and is the highest percentage in the state.

Drilling down deeper, the priciest area in the metro is the new-construction haven of Williamson County. Within the county, College Grove (ZIP code 37046) has the steepest price tags, with a median list price of $3,193,165 and a luxury threshold of $7,209,900.

A full 91% of College Grove's home listings are over one million dollars, behind only Arrington at 96%.

Here, grand estates, often new, boast a median 5,304 square feet of space, significantly larger than the second-place finisher, Nashville (Oak Hill) at 4,015 square feet. It also has the highest per-square-foot price at $578.

"We've always remained in a bubble," says local real estate broker Susan Gregory. "Even when the market turned in 2008, we weren't devastated like the rest of the country. Our new construction kept selling, and we kept building."

She attributes the area's pricing resilience to an excellent public school system, as well as generous estates and sizable plots that lure top earners in numerous industries. Of course, Music City is known for its country crooning residents such as Keith Urban, Faith Hill and Tim McGraw, Jason Aldean, or the late Dolly Parton.

And don't forget those who are still migrating to the Southern state from higher-taxed pastures.

"I just sold a house to a couple from Connecticut, and they are like, 'We just got a huge raise, just in taxes,'" the agent tells Realtor.com. She says that with their move, the couple's property taxes dropped from around $30,000 a year to approximately $8,000.

Such wealthy incomers were mostly responsible for the area's run-up, says the broker.

"They were offering stupid money," she says of pandemic-era buyers who would "overbid" on properties. "Our prices doubled, tripled, and quadrupled."

Around this time, she adds, Williamson County changed its zoning so that subdivision lots had to be at least 5 acres—a common tactic employed to rein in development and protect an area's "character."

"Being on 5 acres increases values significantly," she says.

In Nashville proper, the Oak Hill neighborhood's luxury threshold of $5,815,000 is the second highest in the metro.

While the city remains famous for its music mavens, it is also increasingly a hub for nonmusic industries like healthcare, tech, and even finance.

Business behemoths such as Nissan, In-N-Out Burger, Oracle, and AllianceBernstein have been drawn to the city thanks to low or even no taxes.

High corporate earners are swarming new luxury buildings such as the Four Seasons Private Residences and the Residences at Broadwest, which sits atop the Conrad Nashville, part of the Hilton franchise. At the Four Seasons, which is sold out, price tags range from a hefty $5.16 million to $33.5 million.

In trendy, retail-friendly neighborhood The Gulch, The Residences at The Nashville Edition is being built atop the 261-room Edition hotel.

In the sleek, full-service tower, one-bedroom condos start at $1.62 million and four-bedrooms at $8.65 million.

For Corcoran Reverie agent Kris Wylder, prices like these are on par with Nashville's newish luxury market and scene.

"When I first came here, I thought, 'This city is so undervalued for what it is and what it has to offer,'" she previously told Realtor.com. "It has exploded from an amenity standpoint: the restaurants, the health and wellness options, the shopping. It's just been incredible to see.

"To me, [Nashville] is finally just being valued where it should be. I'm like, 'Oh finally, the prices caught up with everything this city has to offer.'"

Kiri Blakeley writes about trending news at Realtor.com. She has also worked at Forbes Magazine, Forbes.com, CafeMom, and DailyMail.com, covering everything from billionaires to celebrities to crime. #5464. U.S. Home Prices Ticked Up 0.14% in October

U.S. home prices ticked up 0.14% month over month in October on a seasonally adjusted basis. That is the smallest increase in six months.

Prices rose 3.5% from a year earlier in October, the smallest increase since May 2026. Annual price growth has slowed for three straight months.

This is according to the Redfin Home Price Index (RHPI), which uses the repeat-sales pricing method to calculate seasonally adjusted changes in single-family home prices. The RHPI measures how sale prices of homes have changed since their previous sale—similar to the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices—but is reported about a month earlier. October data covers the three months ending October 31, 2026. Read the full RHPI methodology here.

Home prices continued to rise in October, but at a slower pace. Buyers gained more negotiating power than at any point in Redfin’s records, which date back to 2013. Only three of the 50 most populous U.S. metro areas tracked by us were seller’s markets in October.

However, a buyer’s market doesn’t necessarily signal strong buyer’s demand. “Mortgage rates are not that volatile right now, but they’re still higher than they used to be. That’s holding back demand and putting some downward pressure on prices, which have started to fall in many parts of the country,” said Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economics research. “On a national level, we don’t think prices will fall very much.”

There’s also more supply available now, but sellers are not willing to cut prices deeply. “Many sellers are still anchored to the prices they’ve seen over the past few years, and because few sellers are under pressure to sell, that puts a floor under prices,” said Zhao.

Redfin tracks different types of home price trends. While our weekly and monthly housing market reports use the median home-sale price, which has recently shown a decline, the RHPI looks at repeat-sales prices of the same properties over time. It provides that isolates true underlying price appreciation rather than shifts in the types of homes selling, but because this is three-month moving average, it is also a slightly more “backward-looking view” according to Zhao.

Home prices rose in 30 of the 50 major U.S. metros month over month in October.

The biggest increase was in Miami, where home prices rose 1.5% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis. It’s followed by Montgomery County, PA (1.2%), Chicago (1.1%), Pittsburgh (1.0%) and Cincinnati (0.9%).

On a year-over-year basis, prices rose most in San Francisco, up 12.7%. It’s followed by Miami (11.3%), Chicago (9.5%), West Palm Beach (8.9%) and Philadelphia (8.5%).

The biggest price decline was in Seattle (-1.2% month over month). Next come Riverside (-0.7%), Detroit (-0.6%), Las Vegas (-0.6%) and Washington, DC (-0.5%).

Prices declined year over year in six major metros, four in Texas plus Seattle and Phoenix. San Antonio had the biggest drop (-3.0%), followed by Seattle (-2.1%), Dallas (-1.3%) and Austin (-1.1%). Houston (-0.2%) and Phoenix (-0.2%) also declined.

This report is part of Redfin’s monthly Home Price Index series. See all past reports and explore the latest data in the Redfin Data Center.

#5463. New-Home Sales See Welcome Shift, but Not an Overall Improvement

With housing construction continuing to face supply chain and affordability challenges, the latest data from the U.S. Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development saw new-home sales experience a welcome shift upward.

New-home sales jumped 14.2% in October to a rate of 701,000, up from a revised rate of 614,000 in September (originally 676,000). This was also up 7.5% year-over-year.

While a positive shift for the construction industry, the shift is notably due entirely to growth in the South. While all three other regions were down both month-over-month and year-over-year to varying degrees, the South was up 36.2% month-over-month and 24.7% year-over-year.

Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) assistant vice president for forecasting and analysis, noted that while any increase in new-home sales is “encouraging,” it is “too early to interpret the gain as a sustained recovery in housing demand.”

“Elevated mortgage rates and high home prices continue to limit purchasing power, and the outlook for new home sales remains sensitive to financing costs and broader economic conditions,” she continued.

Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant noted that as mortgage rates remain near a three-year high, “the new home industry is experiencing the same pullback in demand that we are seeing on the resale side.”

“While home builders can help offset some of the pain of higher rates by offering buyers rate buydowns and favorable financing, prospective buyers are cautious as we head into the end of 2026,” she continued. “Some buyers have been priced out of the market, while others are simply waiting until 2027, hoping for more favorable conditions.”

Inventory remained on the downslope, falling 1.5% month-over-month and 4.1% year-over-year to 477,000. At the current sales rate, this clocked in at an eight-month supply, down 14% from last month and 11.1% year-over-year.

Builder activity has been significantly diminished due to aforementioned market challenges, with builder confidence recently tanking to a 14-year low.

“Builders are responding with incentives and pricing adjustments, but a more sustained improvement in affordability will be important for strengthening housing demand,” noted NAHB Chairman Bill Owens.

In line with this trend, the median price for a new home slipped 0.3% month-over-month and 3.2 year-over-year to $391,300. Sturtevant noted that this was near a “five year low.”

“Traditionally, new homes command a premium over existing homes, but in October, the median price of a new home was 6% lower than the median price of an existing home,” she continued.”

Sturtevant concluded that with incentives and lower pricing on the table, “new homes continue to be an attractive option for buyers who remain in the market, particularly when builders can offer a discounted interest rate.”

She noted, though, that the issue at hand is “that there are simply fewer buyers in the market as we head into the last few weeks of the year.”

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5462. AI infrastructure stocks continue their slide, but Anthropic closes higher

Investors continued to offload artificial intelligence infrastructure stocks today, but Anthropic PBC recouped some of its losses from earlier this week.

The AI selloff reportedly began in August. It accelerated on Nov. 17, the day Nvidia Corp. CEO Jensen Huang resigned over his affair with a former executive of Megaspeed, a cloud provider under investigation over alleged export control violations. Huang returned to the helm of the chipmaker Monday.

Nvidia closed at $173.73 the day before Huang’s resignation. It dropped as low as $125 during the executive’s two-week hiatus and surged 30% on Monday, the day he returned. Nvidia lost some of its recent gains in today’s trading session: Its share price closed 3.8% lower.

Other AI chip stocks have also taken a hit. Broadcom Inc. closed a small fraction of a percent lower than yesterday, while Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Intel Corp. fell 1.6% and 0.6%, respectively.

The semiconductor stock that logged the biggest drop today is Ambarella Inc., a relatively low-profile maker of AI image analysis chips. Its accelerators are used by edge devices to process footage from their cameras. Ambarella dropped 19.8% today after closing 19% lower yesterday.

The stock’s decline was driven not so much by the broader AI selloff, but rather the weak earnings that Ambarella posted on Tuesday. The company missed expectations across the board. Ambarella said that some customers had canceled or delayed orders to mitigate the financial impact of soaring memory prices.

Micron Inc., one of the world’s top memory chip suppliers, saw its market capitalization drop more than 4.5% today. That’s despite CEO Sanjay Mehrotra’s recent disclosure that the company has already sold out 75% of its 2027 manufacturing capacity. According to the executive, the gap between memory demand and supply is only set to increase next year.

#5460. I Found a Real Estate ‘Unicorn’: 2 Homes, 1 Mortgage, and $187K a Year

Thinking about investing in real estate, but not sure what to buy? Welcome to "My First Deal," where real people spill about how they chose what to invest in, how they found the property, and how that deal is performing. If you have a story to share about your investor journey, email news@realtor.com.

When Steve Kwong ran the numbers on his first traditional investment property, he realized a single broken water heater would wipe out an entire year of profits.

So, the 48-year-old Orlando Realtor® walked away from the deal. Then, he teamed up with a business partner, Rob Leventhal—owner of STR pricing, a revenue management service—and pivoted to short-term rentals.

They searched for three months before buying what Kwong calls a real estate "unicorn": two homes on one lot in Pigeon Forge, TN, with one mortgage. Combined, the two homes grossed $187,000 in 2021—a banner year for most short-term rentals.

Max budget: $475,000Asking price: $479,000Closing price: $462,000Down payment: $92,400Mortgage: $2,390Taxes: $3,040

Originally, I was going to buy a long-term rental on a golf course in Apopka, FL, and would be renting to a friend. I got under contract, but decided not to close. I ran the numbers and would have made $300 a month, which is one capital expense away from not making any money in a year.

I was talking to my friend Rob, who had friends who wanted to buy STRs. This was 2019. We decided to form a partnership and buy something together. We did our research and found Realtor Avery Carl of The Short Term Shop. Everything online led us to buy in the Smoky Mountains—specifically Pigeon Forge, TN.

We relied on Avery to guide us. She advised us that we didn’t want a one- or two-bedroom property. We were looking to spend around $450,000. We were also relying on the data, which told us which parts of town would be good.

Avery and her team did video tours of other homes we were interested in. This was the only one we saw in person.

It was already performing really well. When we were interested in anything, we asked Avery to get the financials to see what the average nightly rate was and what they spent on cleaning. We liked the location. This is down the road from The Island, which is one of the biggest attractions in Pigeon Forge. It also had a private, wooded lot. What drew us to this one most of all was that we were getting two properties on the same lot for one mortgage—it’s a unicorn.

We figured we could bring in higher numbers than what the previous owners had done because we did a lot of research. We had taken a seminar with Richard Fertig and watched all of his videos about how to provide an exceptional guest experience. The industry was at a turning point back then, with people just starting to realize they could do this remotely. We were confident if we implemented all those strategies we would hit a home run.

We offered around $450,000 and settled on $462,000.

We put 20% down. We could have put down less, but we were told that if we ever had to exit in a bad market, we would be at an advantage to sell if we put more down.

From my real estate commissions, and my business partner saved income from his W-2 job (at the time, he worked for a law firm).

As soon as we listed, we got bookings. In the first three months, we made enough to pay the first year of mortgage payments. The first year, we grossed $87,000 and we thought that was good. Our best year was 2021 when we grossed $187,000. The all-in cost to run these for the year is about $45,000 to $50,000, which includes mortgage and expenses. In 2021, that meant bringing in $137,000. That said, we self-manage, so we are not paying 20% to a vacation property manager.

The $187,000 was a [COVID-19] pandemic year, and Tennessee was one of the first states to open. We knew that number wouldn’t be realistic over time. The average gross per year is closer now to $120,000.

You have to continually educate yourself with what is going on in the industry. You will be left behind if you're not up on the newest trends and technology. There is also so much competition.

We hired a VA to help answer messages. At night, we use a little bit of AI.

These two Airbnbs, the four-bedroom and the one-bedroom, helped us save up to buy other properties. We now have four more, including a pool cabin in Gatlinburg, TN, a property in Blue Ridge, GA, and one in Broken Bow, OK.

There are a lot of things I love. Part of it is sentimental because this was our first one. Also, if you’re going to invest in a property, it’s nice to have an asset that you can use and enjoy. You don’t get that with a long-term rental. I never bought any STRs locally because I wanted vacations. I take my brother and his family every year to this property, and that’s the most fun part.

#5459. How State Environmental Laws Are Being ‘Weaponized’ To Stall Housing and Drive Up Costs

Congress is fixated on cutting red tape that drives up the cost of housing—but state policies have a role to play, too, a study finds.

The Pacific Legal Foundation studied state-level policies and found that certain environmental review laws are being "weaponized" to stall developments, driving up the costs and reducing the affordability of housing. This comes as state lawmakers have proposed many new laws this year to curtail policies that stall building, with mixed success.

The study looks at lawsuits that use state environmental policy acts, as well as environmental rights amendments written into state laws. Both of these kinds of disputes are expensive and time-consuming. Developers have to examine and reexamine the environmental impact of developments they want to build, and courts must then determine what cities are required to do to ensure a clean environment for residents.

"A real cost is borne on the people who are renting and buying those homes and apartments," Kyle Sweetland, the study's author, tells Realtor.com®.

About a dozen states have pitched laws that would make it easier to build homes, many of them by reducing zoning or lot size requirements. But some proposals have also met with failure, like California's Proposition 45, which aimed to expedite project reviews through the California Environmental Quality Act.

The Realtor.com Housing Supply Gap research shows the U.S. faces a shortage of 4.03 million homes. Our Let America Build campaign has tracked how states have responded to this shortage, and which are tackling the problem.

California has a long history of slow development on account of environmental review. In one recent example, a 49-unit housing development was stalled for 4.5 years in environmental litigation, which the developer said had raised the cost of the project by $9 million. In another, a 34-home subdivision was stalled for nearly 40 years, in part because of neighbors' environmental concerns.

It's not just a California problem. Sweetland looked at 16 states and the District of Columbia that have environmental policy acts that affect developers, or amendments that affect municipalities. Wyoming, Minnesota, New York, Hawaii, and Massachusetts have both.

But other protections are also in place in California, Nevada, Washington, North Dakota, Illinois, Wyoming, Michigan, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Connecticut, Rhode Island, and the District of Columbia.

It's hard to track precisely how much this kind of litigation drives up the costs of housing. Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner also notes that it's hard to tell how many housing projects didn't start in the first place because developers expected a lawsuit.

"The bigger costs come from what the lawsuit does to the project’s financing and schedule," Berner says. "Appeals typically add years, and in the meantime, most projects can’t secure construction or grant funding. Loans, taxes, and insurance keep accruing, and construction costs can rise while the project waits."

Change could come at the federal level. Last week, the Senate passed a controversial bill that would reduce some federal environmental regulations, like the National Environmental Policy Act, to speed up construction of big-energy projects. Environmental groups opposed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which next heads to the House.

In some instances, the environmental lawsuits don't actually produce better outcomes for the environment. Seattle found that just 16% of cases filed using environmental laws over the 2010s resulted in decisions requiring environmental remediation. In New York, about 22% of cases over 15 years resulted in more environmental reviews, an outside researcher found.

Berner says the balance is that environmental laws are sometimes the easiest avenue residents have to oppose a residential project. It's just a matter of not abusing the process.

"While challenging a project is a relatively cheap thing to do, being on the receiving end of a legal battle can derail a project even without going all the way through the litigation process," Berner says. "This uncertainty adds to the cost of capital for builders and squeezes out lower-margin projects like affordable and infill housing."

Pacific Legal Foundation says one solution for these issues is to narrow the scope of some environmental laws. For instance, Sweetland says legal challenges from outside environmental groups could be limited. That way, the people challenging housing developments have a real vested interest in their outcomes.

He also suggests requirements that groups that lose cases have to pay the legal fees. That isn't typical everywhere, even if developers pay the legal fees when they lose. That provides some incentive that those launching lawsuits have a legitimate claim, as opposed to using the courts as a stalling tactic.

"The law shouldn't just give anybody the ability to have a license to stop a building from moving forward," Sweetland says.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5458. New Haven Weighs Sweeping Ban on Non-Owner-Occupied Airbnb Rentals—Will It Actually Lower Rents?

Homeowners and short-term rental hosts in New Haven, CT, are watching closely as city lawmakers weigh a sweeping proposal that would largely prohibit short-term rentals in the city.

Alderpersons Leland Moore, Frank Douglas, and Mandy Martinelli proposed OR-2026-0039 this past October. The ordinance would bar rentals of 30 days or less in properties that are not a host’s primary residence starting on March 31, 2027. Hosts operating full-time vacation rentals or investor units would need to switch to long-term leases of more than 30 days.

Residents who live in their home could still host short-term stays in their primary residences as long as they obtained a city home-sharing license, remained in the home during the rental, and followed occupancy limits.

"The conversion of long-term residential housing into short-term rentals inflates rental prices, reduces housing inventory, and directly contributes to the displacement of long-term neighbors and residents from communities," the ordinance reads in part.

Supporters of the measure argue it will help free up units in the housing-strapped city. Opponents say it will do little to improve affordability and will hurt residents who make a living from renting out their properties.

At a Nov. 16 Board of Alders meeting where the board was to take a final vote on the measure, more than a hundred residents packed City Hall. Alderman Richard Furlow ultimately tabled the vote until Dec. 7, giving members more time to review proposed amendments to the initiative.

The measure has been supported by housing affordability advocates, hotel and hospitality labor unions, and the city's mayor, Justin Elicker.

"We want to make sure homeowners, if they have an extra room or extra apartment in their building, have the ability to rent," Elicker told NBC affiliate WVIT.  "But at the same time, we're in an affordability crisis right now, and housing affordability is something that's affecting so many New Haven residents. We have a lot of new construction in the city. A lot of that’s affordable, but a lot of that’s not."

The advocacy group New Haven Rising has argued that short-term rentals drive up housing costs for residents and cannibalize local rental stock, keeping locals locked out of homes.

A separate group, Put New Haven First, came out against the proposed ban, noting that the city had yet to complete an economic impact study of the ordinance.

For its part, Airbnb has argued that the proposed ban will hurt locals who make a living by renting out their properties and "puts corporate hotel interests ahead of everyday residents.”

“Airbnb listings make up just 0.5% of the city’s total housing stock," a company spokesperson tells Realtor.com®. "Restricting them won’t lower rents or improve housing availability, but it will take away income that helps local homeowners stay in their homes and supports the house cleaners, landscapers, and small businesses who serve guests.

"Short-term rentals also give visiting families, including those in town for the hospital or university, flexible and affordable places to stay that hotels often can't match," the statement continued. "Residents have asked the Board of Alders to study the impact before acting, and we urge them to look at the evidence before passing a bill that puts corporate hotel interests ahead of everyday residents.”

New Haven is home to Yale University, a world-class hospital system, more than 70 biotech companies, and a burgeoning pizza tourism industry. Locals love its walkability, proximity to nature, and food scene—but they don’t love the city’s struggling housing market.

Between 2020 and 2025, New Haven added 3,535 housing units—more than any other Connecticut city. Yet, the city is still considered one of the worst places in the country for renters. It ranked 138 out of 182 cities on WalletHub's 2026 list of the best places to rent. The city’s median rent is $2,000 a month—more expensive than median rents in 42 of the top 50 metros.

The Realtor.com 2026 Housing Mismatch Report found that New Haven lacks homes for middle-class homebuyers.

"The data makes clear that more inventory alone won’t be enough to unlock the housing market," Danielle Hale, chief economist of Realtor.com, previously said. "A true recovery requires homes at the right price points.”

There are currently 559 rental units available in the city, a 38% increase year over year. By comparison, New Haven has approximately 765 active short-term rental listings across Airbnb, Vrbo, and Booking.com—a 19.1% decrease in active supply compared to October 2025, according to short-term rental tracking site AirDNA.

Proponents of the short-term rental ban have argued that the short-term rentals have had a deleterious effect on the city’s affordability by taking up housing stock that might otherwise be available to locals.

But those 765 units make up just 2% of the city’s 38,621 rental units, according to U.S. Census Bureau data.

What’s more, in other communities where short-term rentals have been curbed or prohibited, the impact on rental prices has been debatable.

In September 2023, New York City implemented Local Law 18, which requires short-term rental hosts to live in the unit and be present during stays. That slashed short-term rental listings by more than 90%, from roughly 38,500 down to around 3,000 to 3,500 registered hosts, according to city reports and a 2026 study.

That study found that the crackdown on short-term rentals had no demonstrable impact on rents and that median monthly rents in Manhattan climbed to a record $4,700 during that period.

A 2024 study from researchers at the College of William & Mary, Purdue University, and Chinese University of Hong Kong examined a similar short-term rental ban in Irvine, CA. According to their research, the ban led to a 23.1% decrease in Airbnb listings and a 2.7% decrease in rental prices.  However, the period of study happened to coincide with the early years of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Residents are eager to hear what amendments to the proposed short-term rental ban the alders will propose at the Dec. 7 meeting.

Sun Queen, a co-founder of Black Lives Matter New Haven and an organizer with the Unhoused Activists Community Team, told the New Haven Independent that short-term rentals can be useful transitional housing for unhoused people.

"I think more time was needed to do more research," she said. "I get it from all angles. We are in a housing crisis.”

Realtor.com reached out to Martinelli, Moore, and Douglas for comment.

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

#5456. Attacker used 1Password employee’s GitHub account to copy customer records

Identity security company 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker, working through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, copied account records belonging to a subset of its customers.

According to the company, the incident came to light on Nov. 19, when 1Password began investigating signs that the GitHub account had been compromised. Using the account, the attacker is said to have pushed malicious code to 1Password’s backend services, which then downloaded what the company describes as “administrative data pertaining to our customers.”

The records taken include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and other non-secret account metadata. Rounding out the list are tokens found in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery.

Customer vaults, the items stored in them and the keys that protect them were not affected, according to 1Password. “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” the company said in its disclosure. Account passwords and Secret Keys are not stored by the company. Also left untouched, the company says, were account recovery keys and the 1Password apps and browser extensions.

Beyond the customer records, the attacker is said to have copied source code from private repositories. Access was also gained to 1Password’s continuous integration and continuous delivery system, which contains infrastructure-related secrets needed for its product to work. According to 1Password, the source code contains no user secrets. Having triggered a rotation of all credentials that may have been exposed, the company claims there has been no impact to its services, availability or product security.

The tokens taken from emailed links cannot be used on their own to access an account, since completing an invitation or recovery also requires a sign-in through single sign-on or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address. Users with provisioning invites or recovery requests pending at the time of the incident, said to be a small number, have been notified directly.

As a precaution, the emailed codes have now been lengthened from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters. 1Password says it has found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed tokens. Other steps taken in response include disabling the affected GitHub account, revoking the stolen token, tightening internal controls and bringing in independent cybersecurity experts to validate its containment and remediation work.

Customers do not need to change anything in their 1Password accounts. The company is instead warning users to be cautious of phishing attempts, such as unexpected emails, texts or calls about invitations or account recovery requests they did not start. “1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key,” the company noted.

1Password, which claims to serve more than 200,000 businesses, did not say how many customers had records downloaded. How the employee’s GitHub account was compromised was also left unexplained.

This is not the first intrusion 1Password has disclosed. In October 2023, the company said that an attacker had accessed its Okta tenant using session data stolen in the breach of Okta Inc.’s customer support system. No user data was found to have been compromised in that case.

Today’s disclosure comes nearly four years after rival password manager LastPass US LP revealed that a hacker had copied encrypted customer password vaults, using information taken in an earlier breach of its development environment.

1Password says it will update its post if the investigation turns up anything that changes what it has disclosed so far.

#5455. Hawaii Beachfront Battle Turns Ugly as Neighbor Blames 7-Home Project for Floodwater Boils

What was supposed to be a routine permit hearing for seven new homes on Oahu’s North Shore devolved into a bitter clash, with neighbors alleging unpermitted construction, threatened ancestral burial sites, and tainted runoff one blames for giving local children boils.

“It’s a disgrace to the community,” Carla Lenhoff, who lives on the same residential lane as the proposed development, told Honolulu planners. “It’s a disgrace to the ocean. It’s a disgrace to your neighbors.”

At the center of the Nov. 20 town hall was homeowner Linda Donoso and Malaekahana LLC’s application for a Special Management Area permit on Mālaekahana Bay—a quiet stretch of coastline lined with beachfront homes between Kahuku and Lāʻie.

According to the public hearing notice, the permit would cover construction of seven new homes on Condominium Property Regime (CPR) Units 2 through 8, with the existing home retained on CPR Unit 1. The request also includes installation of six individual wastewater systems and utility connections, plus driveways, walkways, fencing, rock walls, and other site improvements.

The property is divided into eight separately owned condominium units, but Honolulu treats them as a single lot for zoning purposes.

Donoso said she took on the cost of pursuing a coastal permit covering seven additional homes because the other owners were unwilling to pay.

Donoso, who has lived on Unit 1 since 2016, acquired Unit 6 two years later.

“I am not a developer, I am building a home for my family. In order for me to build on this property, a legal CPR, I have to apply for an SMA permit,” Donoso told Realtor.com® ahead of the hearing.

“It will benefit all the lot owners. But in order for me to build, I have to pay for this SMA because no one else is.”

Donoso, who lost her husband to COVID-19 and wants her family nearby, told Realtor.com that there was no existing home on that lot, but one of those homes was already standing, unfinished, on a unit owned by her son, Allen Graham.

Michael Marchak, the city planner reviewing the application, confirmed that an August citation for building without a permit remained open.

Neighbors weren't swayed by Donoso’s description of the project.

“Are we just going to short-term rent it out to as many people as possible?” Lenhoff asked.

While Kahuku remains mostly residential, it sits along Oahu’s popular North Shore tourism corridor, where an estimated 12,100 visitors were present on a typical day in 2024, according to Hawaii state tourism research.

For Naomi Fiatoa-Holani, who raised six children along the same lane and was baptized in the bay, the prospect of additional vacation rentals hit close to home.

“We purposely live there for the serenity and the culture of that area,” she told planners.

In fact, short-term vacation rentals are already prohibited in the area. City zoning rules bar owners from renting out the homes for stays of fewer than 30 consecutive days, regardless of the coastal permit.

And Donoso had previously been cited over short-term rental advertising.

The city cited her home on Unit 1 in December 2023 over an ad offering stays under 30 days. Donoso acknowledged renting to vacationers, but insists she stopped accepting bookings after that notice.

A second citation followed in April 2024 over a recurring ad. Both cases are now marked corrected and closed by the city, and at the hearing, Donoso disputed that she had resumed renting out her property.

She also rejected the suggestion that the proposed development would become an outpost for tourists. Her son owned Unit 2, she told planners, and her grandson had recently bought Unit 4.

“It isn’t going to be a vacation rental community,” she said.

But neighbors questioned whether they could trust the applicants to follow the rules when construction on Graham’s home on Unit 2 had already begun without a permit.

Honolulu's Aug. 13 violation notice documented the unpermitted construction of a two-story structure. Neighbors alleged that work continued even after crews were told to stop, though city officials did not establish whether that was the case at the hearing.

“They’re still building,” Lenhoff told planners, adding that she had submitted photographs.

That incident was particularly troubling to residents because of the significance of the ground on which the home stands.

“That’s precious to us,” Fiatoa-Holani said of the sand along the bay. “That’s where our kūpuna are buried.”

In Native Hawaiian tradition, ancestral remains, known as iwi kūpuna, are sacred, representing an enduring spiritual connection between the land, the deceased, and their living descendants.

And in 2018, human remains were discovered during construction of two homes in a neighboring three-home development, according to draft minutes of the Oahu Island Burial Council.

No one at the hearing reported finding remains on Graham's unit, nor had archaeologists found cultural resources during an earlier investigation of the property—but that investigation had its limits.

The archaeologists dug six test trenches in 2021, none on Graham's unit. The applicants' own filing acknowledges that the State Historic Preservation Division considered the findings insufficient to rule out impacts to buried cultural resources.

The agency requested on-site archaeological monitoring during ground-disturbing work, noting that the area's sandy soils are known to contain human remains.

Graham maintained that work on his house had involved little new excavation. He said sand used behind a retaining wall came from an earlier driveway excavation.

“We didn’t go deep below the surface,” he said.

But when public testimony ended, Marchak asked whether anyone had monitored construction on Unit 2 for archaeological finds.

Donoso said the family had tried to arrange it.

“We couldn’t get it done till January,” she said.

Neighbors also raised concerns about water quality, describing floodwater they feared was carrying contaminants from the property onto their shared lane.

Fiatoa-Holani described watching water and debris wash down the road her children walked to collect the mail. She believed the flooding had made local children sick, and that wading through the water had given them boils.

Other residents also complained about runoff, though Fiatoa-Holani was the only one who reported children developing boils.

"It was completely dry during the rain,” she said, adding that her grandchildren had never developed any symptoms.

The permit application likewise maintains that the property's permeable sandy soil would keep stormwater on-site, with dry wells proposed to help manage drainage.

But beyond the dispute over flooding was another question: Could the property accommodate wastewater from eight homes?

The plans call for six wastewater systems, with Units 3 and 4 sharing one and Units 7 and 8 sharing another. Donoso said her son had already replaced an old cesspool on Unit 2 with a septic system.

Lenhoff challenged whether the parcel had enough land for the six proposed systems; and in his final questions to the applicants, Marchak raised the same issue.

Under state rules, six systems would require 60,000 square feet of land. The property originally measured 64,033 square feet, but a 2015 certified shoreline survey documented 6,229 square feet lost to erosion.

That leaves 57,804 square feet in the application's calculations—2,196 square feet short of the stated requirement.

When Marchak asked whether the wastewater plans had been submitted to the state Department of Health, Roy Irei, the applicants' engineer, said he had discussed the proposal with officials but had yet to submit it for approval.

Kahuku resident Evelyn Lane had a more immediate request for the unfinished house already standing behind Donoso's home.

“They should tear down the unpermitted building that they built, and I don’t know why that wasn’t brought up in this discussion,” Lane told planners.

Three days later, Hawaii News Now was interviewing Lenhoff about the project when Donoso stepped in.

“So you guys want to fight, you guys will have a fight,” Donoso told the neighbors. The station reported that the argument lasted roughly 20 minutes and ended after police were called.

Donoso told the station her son hadn't known he needed a building permit and that the house was “already done by the time he was notified.”

The October application anticipates construction beginning in early 2027, with work on Donoso's own home scheduled for the fourth quarter of that year. The full project is expected to take approximately five years after permits are approved.

First, however, the City Council must decide whether to grant the coastal permit.

Under Honolulu law, planners have 45 days after the hearing to send their recommendation to the City Council, unless the applicant agrees to an extension. Residents will have another opportunity to testify when the City Council takes up the proposal, though no date has been announced.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5454. Yearly Inflation Measures Still Hot; Economics Professor Deems December Rate Hike ‘A Done Deal’

The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, released monthly by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), showed an increase of 0.3% in October. The PCE price index gained 0.5% in September, making October a very slight cooldown.

The “core” PCE price index, or the PCE price index with food and energy data excluded, held steady at a 0.3% month-to-month increase.

The PCE price index is widely considered to be the Fed’s favored measure of inflation, and thus a cooldown in PCE price index gains may also signal a cooldown in Fed rate hikes.

The year-to-year data, however, point in the opposite direction. Compared to October of last year, the PCE price index actually increased 3.8%, a 0.2% gain from the same year-to-year comparison in October.

The Core PCE price index also shot up 3.3% compared to October of last year. Navy Federal Chief Economist Heather Long called this “(a)nother hot inflation reading” on X and remarked that “Core came in hotter than expected. It’s yet another reminder that the inflation problem right now goes beyond a mere energy shock.”

University of Pennsylvania Economics Professor Mohamed A. El-Erian made the implications of the PCE report very clear in a post on X: “All this will leave markets feeling that a Fed rate hike on December 9th is essentially a done deal, disappointing those who were hoping for a quick repeat of 2018.”

A Fed rate hike in December is likely disheartening news for the housing market, which has already seen a “crater(ing)” of pending home sales due to a high October spike in mortgage rates.

Rates have already edged down (and back up again, albeit remaining lower than the highest of the October highs), but anticipation of a rate hike may not grant buyers the confidence needed to reenter the market.

In other news, though, the latest BEA report also recorded a current-dollar PCE rise of 0.3% in October, the equivalent of $63.8 billion. The increase in expenditures is downstream of increased spending on goods and services, in which the BEA’s category of “other nondurable goods” represented the highest increase. Motor vehicles and parts experienced the largest decrease.

Lastly, personal income increased $201.8 billion or 0.7% month-over-month. According to the report, this increase mostly reflected increases in compensation, government social benefits and personal income receipts on assets.

Audrey Jiang is an editorial intern for RISMedia.

#5453. ‘Momentum is the cure of all fear’: Mauricio and Alexia Umansky talk ‘Special Forces’

Jumping out of a helicopter into water below, rappelling down a 22-story building, enduring chemical warfare gas exposure — if you’ve never seen Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test, these are just a few of the tasks that must be completed.

It’s a reality TV show in which celebrities do physical challenges from the actual Special Forces selection process playbook. It’s like a competition show, but there are no eliminations, and no one gets voted off.

To leave, participants must voluntarily withdraw, be medically withdrawn by a DS (directing staff) due to injury or be dismissed for refusing a direct order. During the final test, the DS ejects those who fail the interrogation or selection test.

Season 5 is set in the Malaysian jungle. It features Candace Cameron Bure, Brandi Glanville, Oliver Hudson, Ruby Rose, George Santos, Bre Tiesi, Matt Barnes, and Mauricio and Alexia Umansky, among others.

At the time that this article was published, Alexia was still in the competition. Mauricio voluntarily withdrew after a rib injury sustained during a hand-to-hand fighting challenge with former NBA player Matt Barnes. Mauricio said the injury took two or three months to heal.

The following challenge involved gas, and Mauricio didn’t think his ribs could take it. He said he feared having a bad lung injury in the Malaysian jungle. Alexia agreed with the decision, saying the gas was the “most painful thing” she’d ever experienced in her life.

Inman spoke to Mauricio and Alexia midway through the season about the experience, the latest industry news and what’s next for The Agency.

What follows is the conversation, edited for length and clarity.

I think for me, 100 percent, the heat. I think I anticipated intense heat and intense humidity, but you don’t know what it’s like until you really feel it … It was so unbearably hot, and in our barracks that we slept in, there was no windows, and when you were inside, you actually couldn’t tell like what was even happening out there. But it was almost like … “Good, let me be locked in this metal box because the outside is crazy.”

Mauricio: I think for me, it was just the intensity of what a jungle really is. The first day we got there … when we were all showering and waiting to shower, there was a scorpion crawling on my leg, about to go in my boot, which I felt it and took it off just in the nick of time. Because if it went in my boot, it would have stung me, no question, right?

Alexia: It’s so hard to choose because literally every single thing was hard. Part of me wanted to say the car rides leading up to each challenge, because we didn’t know what was coming, and it was always so intense in the car. My heart would start pounding … the bottom line is the hardest part is just making sure that your mindset is correct [in] doing all these things and waking up each day and moving forward because that’s really what gets going is just moving forward and choosing to keep on going.

Mauricio: Yeah, I think Alexia nailed it. I mean, for me, it was really all about the little victories. The only way to survive is by looking at small victories, small steps … we used to say just make it to the next meal, just make it to the next day, just make it to tonight.

For me, the hardest part was leaving, was having to voluntarily withdraw. I did not want to have a medical withdrawal, so I didn’t want to go see the doctor and have them withdraw me.

Mauricio: Not one thing for me. What about you, Alexia?

Alexia: No. There’s nothing about this that’s easy.

Alexia: We loved everybody so much. I mean, we still talk all the time, and we still love each other so much. The words of affirmation we all told each other to this day are so special … But I think my first answer would have to be Candace [Cameron] Bure … she’s so strong, and we got looped together for a bunch of things because of our height similarities.

Mauricio: Well, I have to say that the person who surprised me the most was Alexia … the strength of her mind, her strength and what she did was extraordinary.

Alexia: Oh my god, yeah. Are you kidding me? All the time.

Alexia: Definitely thought it was pretty cool. It was an honor to be punched in the chest by DJ Tanner … I actually appreciated very much that she didn’t hold back because I just felt like I was treated like an equal, an individual.

Alexia: I’ve never punched anyone or anything … the second she threw the first punch, I knew she was so much stronger than me. But my goal was to just not fall down. I really didn’t want to fall down, so I was just trying to stay up the entire time. It felt like a fight went on for so long.

Alexia: I had zero plans on talking about that while we were there. Before we go into the course, they make you talk to some psychologists … they do ask you before the show, “What’s the worst thing that you’ve ever been through?”

And I remember thinking, like, “Are we gonna go there? … That would be so inappropriate. Everything’s in my power, and I’m not gonna go there” … Once I was finally in there, I understood why they asked … you’re stripped down to the very core of you, and you’re tired, and you’re pushing yourself, and you’re emotional, you’re exhausted … And Bre Tiesi, she got emotional, and [she said to me] ”I haven’t cried in years. I hate crying.”

It was really about discovering and repurposing the strength that I always felt that I had, but there was a time that I had felt that I had lost that.

And each night, as I was going to sleep, I just remember thinking to myself, “This is so rewarding, and this is so empowering, and this is so incredible for someone that has gone through what I have” … some people [feel like they] get their voice back. I always felt like I had my voice, but I feel like I got to discover a strength I always knew I had that someone had pushed me to question, and feeling that was just incredibly healing.

Alexia: No, not my parents. I had told two of my sisters before, and then, obviously, I told my dad on the course, and then, before the show aired, I ended up calling my mom and [sister] Portia to tell them because I obviously did not want that to be the first time they read it. And even though I spoke about it on the course, I’m still very, very afraid to tell them afterward, too.

Mauricio: It was extremely difficult … I was just proud of Alexia every single day, every single moment … hearing that story was just another revelation of her conquering and finally talking about something that I wish she never held back … I just wanted to reach out and just hug her. But by the same token, I also wanted to give her space and let her be her in that moment that she was sharing with everybody. So there was like a lot of stuff going through my mind.

There was anger toward this kid that did this … But [watching her let go of it] was beautiful to watch … from my perspective, it was like, “Do I reach over and become a dad and just give her a big hug, or do I let her go through this moment, psychologically speaking, of letting it all come out?”

And I was just proud of her all the way around.

In hindsight, I love that she was able to share that, get it off her chest with us, with everybody, with the world. I think it’s super powerful.

Yes, I live by a lot of different small philosophies. Certainty versus doubt. Momentum is the cure of all fears. All of these are the different things where you just have to move forward, right? In order to accomplish something, you kind of just have to move forward, right? … the moment that I went from being an agent to opening up a brokerage, you jump off the cliff; you hope the parachute catches.

To today … here we are in a really difficult real estate market. I mean, it is not fun out there right now whatsoever. Yet [The Agency is] still growing. We’re still putting money out there. We’re still doing things right. So yeah, to me that’s just a philosophy that I always live by.

Mauricio: I don’t know. We’ll just keep going. I really like that show Traitors. I would love to be on that show. That could be a fun one for me, so I’m putting that out into the universe.

Alexia: My dream would be to do a reality TV show with my family … We did Buying Beverly Hills, and we’ve done Real Housewives for like [16] years now. But we’ve never done something all of us together, just us, and I think that’ll be really cool.

Mauricio: I’m going to leave that one on the table. If anything, it’s for 2030. There’s still plenty of time to do that and make that decision. But I love LA, and I think I can help LA a lot. I think we live in an amazing city, and if the moment comes, and I’m set up in the right position in the business and I feel like I can actually win, I might do it. But I wouldn’t do it if I didn’t feel like I could actually win.

Mauricio: It’s an absolute mess, what’s going on in our in our in our industry right now, particularly with the listings. My take is, it’s quite simple. I think that there’s a lot of change that’s happening. I believe that it’s somewhere in the middle. Like I do everything.

I believe sellers should have choice, but I believe that we should be sharing those private listings amongst everybody — every agent, every brokerage firm, not just keeping it for themselves. I feel like there’s a lot happening right now in the industry where everybody’s really looking out for themselves: the MLSs, NAR, Compass.

Actually, Compass, I think, wants to collaborate, wants to share, but they’re in a big, big fight. But in the meantime, this Clear Cooperation Policy is what is allowing them to keep all the listings to themselves and not share them … The PLS is exactly what that was, and I still think that if Clear Cooperation Policy didn’t pass, it would have been an amazing business to have right now.

Mauricio: We are really positioned as the premier luxury brokerage firm outside of Compass right now. They’ve got Sotheby’s, they’ve got Christie’s, they’ve got all of those different brands, and we’re the only independent luxury brokerage firm out there right now.

So I’m excited to be in that position. Competitors make you better every single day … I’m excited in terms of where we sit, where we stand in a very difficult time; I’m not excited about the market. We really need to do some things to improve it. We’ve had three years of very, very difficult conditions, and it’s going to be very difficult for people to survive. And those that do survive will come out better.

I think we’re in a good position to survive, but we’ve got our work cut out for us over the next year, year and a half. But we’ll continue to grow. We’ll continue to expand, and I’m excited to just be a part of this industry. But man, it’s hard out there right now.

#5452. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

Here’s the usual scenario: You sign up for a coaching program. You’re excited, and you should be. Everybody wants to feel a little less alone in a job you mostly do by yourself, in your car.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

#5451. Bellflower Rents Are Skyrocketing—but Is It Worth Trying to Buy in Los Angeles ?

According to the latest Realtor.com® Rent report, the rental market is showing signs of a shift. October 2026 marked the first month of year-over-year rent growth since June 2023, though the change was modest. The median national asking rent rose by just $1, a 0.1% increase from the previous year, to $1,692.

Additionally, the Housing Vacancy Survey revealed that the rental vacancy rate hit 7.6% in the last quarter, the highest it has been since early 2014. In the Los Angeles market, rents can vary dramatically, from the high $1000s to as much as $6000 in more exclusive neighborhoods.

Which brings us to Bellflower, a neighborhood where the cost of renting has its own unique story.

In Bellflower, the average rent has been on the rise. The average rent increased from $2,439 in the second quarter of 2026 to $2,551 in the third quarter. This represents an increase of $112 per month.

Furthermore, this monthly increase adds up over time, costing renters an additional $1,344 per year. Then again,  for those considering buying, the median listing price for a home in Bellflower was $699,500 in October 2026.

According to the latest L.A. Rental Report, the median asking rent for all properties in Los Angeles County was $2,554 in the third quarter of 2026, a decline of 3.6% from the previous year. Despite this county-wide dip, buying a home remains significantly more expensive. A median-priced home cost $4,716 more per month than renting, which is nearly 185% higher, making the decision to save money by renting a compelling one for many, even with a hefty down payment and a friendly landlord.

Renters may be catching a break, as homeownership in L.A. County remains out of reach for many. With mortgage rates still above 7%, higher borrowing costs could push the dream of buying even further away for those currently renting apartments. This situation may give tenants some leverage when it comes to their lease.

If you're looking to negotiate a rent decrease, consider asking your landlord what they might accept in exchange for a lower monthly payment. This could include offering to sign a longer lease, providing a higher security deposit, or prepaying a month or two of rent. Being a reliable and considerate tenant is also a strong bargaining chip.

"The best way I’ve seen renters negotiate rent is to be an amazing applicant," said Glenn Carter, a real estate investor at Condo Capital. Remind your landlord that you consistently pay on time, maintain the property well, and are considerate of your neighbors.

Moreover, landlords often value stability and may be willing to negotiate to keep a good tenant. "As a landlord, I would accept lower rent from a dependable source," said Steve Silberberg, a Boston -based landlord.
