#5376. Who should referee a national MLS, brokers or a neutral body?

The piece supports national listing standardization but opposes a broker-controlled system. It argues the operator should be neutral, like payment networks, to protect competition and limit reliance on private channels.  AI Summary

When Open Real Estate was announced, the question of a national listing system moved back to the center of our industry. I am early in my read on this particular initiative. But I have spent a long time on the underlying question, enough that I have written a white paper of more than 70 pages on why a broker-controlled national MLS is the wrong design and what a right one would look like. For the leaders reading this, I want to lay out the core of that thinking, because this is a decision our industry may actually make in the next few years, and we should make it with our eyes open.

First, credit where it is due. A coalition of large brokerages banded together and put their names to a public position. That takes coordination and conviction, and it is plainly a response to a real and growing trend, the migration of listings into private and exclusive channels that never touch the open market. The concern is legitimate. When inventory moves into walled gardens, buyers see less, agents compete on access instead of expertise, and the consumer is quietly disadvantaged. Leaders who are worried about that are worried about the right thing.

I see two problems, one practical and one structural, and the structural one is the one that should concern every leader who does not run one of the three or four largest firms in the country.

The practical problem is straightforward. The founders have said that Open Real Estate is not a national MLS and is not meant to replace local MLSs. Whatever we call it, it is built to function as shared national listing infrastructure, and that infrastructure includes a participant view option, where a listing can be seen only by agents at participating brokerages and cannot be publicly marketed by anyone. In other words, the model does not stop private listings. It gives them a larger, better-organized home. The exact behavior this is meant to counter can continue, and we have built a bigger shared system that still has walls inside it.

Consider the architecture we have now. Hundreds of local MLSs operate across the country. We complain about that fragmentation endlessly, and it does create real friction for agents and consumers. But the fragmentation also delivers a benefit almost no one names. Each MLS acts as its own silo, its own firewall. Because the data lives in hundreds of independent repositories, no single company controls the national market. There is a series called Silo that captures the idea well. Each silo runs itself, and no one can command the whole system. Our MLS structure has handed us that same protection almost by accident. The walls are inconvenient, and the walls are also the reason no one firm owns the country’s data.

Now collapse all of it into one national system, whatever label it carries, and ask the only question that matters. Who runs it? If the answer is that brokers run it, then the brokers with the deepest pockets will control the nation’s listing infrastructure. The independents, the single-office shops, the regional firms, they will have little to no voice. Whoever sits atop a broker-controlled national system writes the rules for everyone downstream, including their direct competitors. That is not a free market with shared plumbing. That is a tollgate owned by a few, and everyone else pays to pass through.

Powerfact: Whoever controls a national MLS controls the terms of competition for every agent in the country. That cannot be a competitor.

So, let me be clear that I am not against unification. A national MLS done correctly would be a real asset. It would let an agent see listings nationwide rather than stitching together access market by market. It would mean one playbook, the same rules, forms, and fields in every state, so practicing across state lines or relocating would not require relearning the mechanics each time. That consistency would benefitagents, brokers, and consumers. The debate should not be unify or do not unify. The fight is already here, and it should be about who holds the technology in the middle.

And we already have a proven answer inside our own economy. Visa and MasterCard.

The first bank card came from Bank of America. When other banks saw it working, each began building its own card and its own processing, and the result was chaos, because every bank set different rules and the consumer experience depended on which card you carried. The resolution was not to let the largest bank operate everyone else’s cards. It was Visa, a separate entity sitting in the middle. Each bank still runs its own business and competes on its own terms. The technology and the standards that make the system uniform for the consumer are handled by a neutral party that no single bank owns.

That is the template for a national MLS. Not control by the largest brokerages, but a neutral, broker-independent organization that operates the technology and maintains uniform rules, while every brokerage, large and small, continues to run its own business and compete on skill and service. Keep each firm a silo where it should be a silo. Make the shared rails in the middle belong to no one in particular. That is the only structure that stays fair to the smallest independent and the largest franchise at the same time.

When the next national platform is announced, and there will be more of them, do not evaluate it on the feature list. Evaluate it on governance. Ask who owns it, who sits on the board, how the rules get changed, and what recourse a small brokerage has if the controlling firms decide to change the terms. If the governance concentrates power in a handful of competitors, the convenience on the surface is not worth the dependency underneath. If the governance looks like Visa, neutral, independent, and accountable to all participants rather than to the biggest ones, then we may finally have something worth building.

I appreciate the effort behind Open Real Estate, and I share the concern that prompted it. But good intentions do not fix bad architecture. A national listing system run by brokers would trade the problem of private listings for the larger problem of a privatized commons, owned by the few and rented to the many. We can do better, and we have a model sitting in our wallets that shows us how. Build the referee first. Then build the league.

Darryl Davis, CSP, is a national speaker, real estate coach, and the bestselling author of How to Become a Power Agent® in Real Estate. Learn more at darrylspeaks.com.

#5375. Beyond Nvidia: Convoy co-founder and former Microsoft leader raise $277M to rethink AI infrastructure

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 4:30 amNovember 23, 2026 at 1:27 pm

Former Microsoft executives Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan have raised $277 million on a bet that the next wave of AI will run on a very different kind of data center.

The outsized seed funding for their new startup, Marlowe, reflects the scale of the challenge they’re taking on. As AI shifts from training models to running them in everyday products, Marlowe designs and operates computing systems for that work. It’s starting with chips from AMD and Etched, expanding beyond the Nvidia GPUs that have fueled the AI boom.

They say tuning the chips, networking and software for specific AI workloads and applications will maximize performance and efficiency, lowering costs as a result.

The new funding values Marlowe at $1.15 billion, according to the company, making it a unicorn out of the gate. Accel led the latest round, joined by a long list of big names in tech and finance, from KKR co-founder Henry Kravis to Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Lewis, Marlowe’s CEO, previously co-founded the trucking startup Convoy and later was an enterprise AI leader at Microsoft, where Srinivasan, now Marlowe’s CTO, was a corporate vice president and the company-wide technical lead for AI infrastructure.

“The demand for intelligence and AI is very high,” Lewis said in an interview, when asked how a former freight marketplace CEO ended up in AI computing. “It’s something that should be accessible and affordable for everyone.”

Marlowe, founded in May, is based in both Bellevue, Wash., and Redwood City, Calif., and is approaching 30 employees. Lewis said the two home bases reflect where its customers, partners and talent are concentrated, pointing to Bellevue as an emerging AI hub.

Lewis, a former Amazon general manager, joined Flexport as a technical advisor when the freight company acquired Convoy’s technology after the startup’s abrupt shutdown in 2023. In February 2025, he returned to Microsoft, where he had also worked previously, as a chief product officer focused on enterprise AI, later becoming a corporate vice president.

GeekWire first reported in June that he had left Microsoft to launch a new startup, but he wasn’t ready to share details at the time.

From Microsoft to Marlowe: The founders said the idea for Marlowe grew out of what they saw at Microsoft: demand was surging for inference, running AI models in products and services, but data centers were still being built mainly for training those models in the first place.

“We were always oversold, effectively sold out,” Lewis said.

Since then, demand for inference has grown faster than supply, pushing up costs at the same time that power shortages, permitting and financing are making new data centers harder to build. The company cites a 40% increase in data center construction costs since 2020, which makes every watt more valuable.

The company isn’t using Nvidia chips for now, but it hasn’t ruled them out.

Its first site, built around Etched’s chips, is scheduled to go live in December, the founders said. A second, larger site using AMD’s new Helios systems is on track for the second quarter of 2027.

Both sites are under contract, and a third is under a letter of intent. The company says it has signed three customer agreements but isn’t yet naming the customers or the locations.

Srinivasan said that at the big tech companies where he has worked, chips from vendors other than Nvidia made up a small slice of the fleet. When a new AI model came out, the top engineers focused on getting it running on the Nvidia chips, and the rest got left behind.

“There were literally times when a significant portion of our non-Nvidia fleet was either idle or grossly underused or didn’t support the latest models and workloads,” he said.

That’s the gap Marlowe is trying to close. Its engineers work directly on customers’ workloads to get other chips performing at their full potential, giving those companies a way to reduce their dependence on a single supplier.

Marlowe says gains of 10% to 20% at each layer of the system, from chips and networking to power management and software, add up to two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds, measured in tokens, the chunks of text that AI models process and generate.

Competition and funding: Marlowe isn’t alone in the bet. Gimlet Labs, which raised $300 million at a $3 billion valuation in September, and General Compute, which raised $100 million in October, are also building inference clouds that run on a mix of chips.

CoreWeave, the largest of the so-called neoclouds, rents out computing power built almost entirely on Nvidia chips. Nvidia held about 47 million CoreWeave shares as of Sept. 30, and CoreWeave has taken on about $47 billion in debt to build out its data centers.

Marlowe’s launch also comes during a turbulent stretch for Nvidia. The company’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on Monday, less than two weeks after his resignation.

Much of Marlowe’s funding will go toward chips, networking equipment and the support needed to run the sites, along with hiring, the founders said. By the standards of AI infrastructure, $277 million doesn’t go far.

Rather than chasing giant facilities, Marlowe plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts and then finance more capacity site by site, Lewis said. He noted that some startups have raised four to five times as much and will deploy a little less computing power on a similar timeline.

The $277 million includes a smaller initial round led by Eclipse, Lewis said. Eclipse founder and CEO Lior Susan is Marlowe’s executive chairman, and Ido Susan, founder and CEO of the data center networking company DriveNets, is on the board. Other backers include Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Journey and Valor.

Angel investors also include Box CEO Aaron Levie and former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky. Mark Okerstrom, the former Expedia CFO and CEO who later served as Convoy’s president, is also an investor.

Past lives: Srinivasan’s career runs from video games to AI infrastructure. In an earlier stint at Microsoft, he worked on DirectX and games including Halo 3, then spent eight years at Valve, where he led the team that built the first Steam mobile app.

He later served as the lead architect for machine learning training infrastructure at Facebook, and as a technical fellow at LinkedIn before moving to Microsoft’s CoreAI group in 2025.

Marlowe is a very different business from Convoy, the digital freight marketplace Lewis co-founded to match truckers with shippers. Convoy reached a $3.8 billion valuation before shutting down in 2023, amid a freight recession and a pullback in venture funding.

Asked how Marlowe would avoid getting similarly squeezed by forces outside its control in a capital-intensive business, Lewis said the industry is at “the very beginning” of a long-term shift in how people use AI and data.

He also pointed to a mix of long- and short-term contracts and multiple customers, rather than one big customer that could pull out.

Ultimately, Lewis said he believes Marlowe’s edge will come down to having the engineering skills to get the most out of new chips. “You can’t just take a new chip that comes out and plug it in and expect it to produce tokens,” he said. “You have to go do the work.”

#5374. Dance Experts Serge and Yana Nelyubov Explain What Happens at Your First Ballroom Lesson

Serge and Yana Nelyubov outline what beginners can expect during their first ballroom dance lesson and how instructors help build confidence from the start.

WILLIAMSVILLE, N.Y., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What happens at your first ballroom lesson? A new HelloNation article featuring insights from Dance Experts Serge and Yana Nelyubov of Fred Astaire Buffalo in Williamsville, New York, explains what beginners can expect during their first visit to a dance studio and how ballroom dance lessons are designed to create a relaxed, welcoming learning experience.

The article explains that many first-time students arrive with questions about what they will be asked to do and whether previous experience is required. According to the feature, beginner ballroom dancing is designed with new dancers in mind, allowing students to learn at a comfortable pace without feeling pressured to keep up with anyone else.

Readers learn that a first ballroom lesson typically begins with a conversation between the student and the dance instructor. This discussion helps the instructor understand each student's goals, whether they are preparing for a wedding, looking for a new hobby, or simply interested in learning ballroom dance lessons for fun. The article notes that understanding these goals allows instruction to be tailored to each student's comfort level.

The feature also emphasizes that no prior dance experience is necessary. Many students arrive for their first ballroom lesson without knowing any dance steps, and instructors expect beginners to start from the basics. According to the article, lessons are structured to introduce simple movements one at a time, helping students develop confidence as each new skill builds naturally on the last.

The article explains that early instruction often focuses on fundamental skills such as footwork, rhythm, posture, balance, and partner connection. These concepts provide the foundation for future ballroom dance lessons while remaining approachable for new students. By introducing these basics gradually, instructors help students feel successful from the very beginning.

Readers also learn that students can participate whether they arrive with a partner or attend alone. The article explains that many dance studios provide instructors or practice partners when needed, allowing anyone interested in beginner ballroom dancing to participate comfortably. This flexibility helps make ballroom dancing accessible to a wide range of students.

Another point highlighted in the article is that making mistakes is an expected part of learning. The dance instructor encourages questions, provides corrections, and allows students time to practice without feeling rushed. Rather than viewing mistakes as setbacks, the article describes them as valuable opportunities that help students improve with each lesson.

The feature also discusses the pace of instruction during a first ballroom lesson. Instead of introducing numerous dances at once, instructors typically focus on mastering a few basic movements correctly before moving forward. This steady approach helps students retain what they have learned while building confidence through consistent progress.

The article also offers practical guidance about preparing for the lesson itself. Comfortable clothing that allows easy movement and secure shoes are generally all that is needed for a first visit to a dance studio. Special dance attire is rarely necessary, allowing beginners to focus on learning rather than worrying about what to wear.

As the lesson concludes, many students discover they have learned more than they expected in a single session. The article notes that initial nervousness often gives way to confidence as basic movements become more familiar. Regular ballroom dance lessons continue to build on that foundation, helping students develop new skills while enjoying the movement, social connection, and satisfaction that come with steady improvement.

#5373. Jensen Huang returns, but controversies keep growing around Nvidia

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

Jensen Huang’s back, and not everyone is happy with that.

Nvidia’s board reversed the resignation of its former and current-again CEO Monday, apparently under pressure from the well-known business genius and lame-duck President Donald Trump, who worried that the stock market and the AI trade would suffer without him at the helm.

Huang (pictured) clearly has management talent, having built one of the most valuable companies in the world. But his return, amid continuing revelations and questions about Nvidia’s business, sets an awful precedent in business. No one person should be too important to fail, and Huang set up a corporate structure that courts disaster if he’s forced to leave again or gets run over by a bus. That’s a world-class failure of a CEO and his board at one of their most basic jobs, and his tech-bro enablers should know better than to clamor for his return.

After all, internal and government investigations continue, as more details come to light about probably the worst of the whole affair(s). It’s clear that at a time when there’s existential worry about China closing the U.S. lead in AI — a potential defense and cybersecurity disaster — the chief supplier of AI chips was allowing cutting-edge chips to be sent to China. Oh, and this week’s stock market pretty much discounted much of the supposed benefit Huang’s reinstatement was supposed to provide.

So what are we left with? The CEO of the pivotal company in AI is back with not even a slap on the wrist, let alone any consequences for multiple affairs — one with a woman who shuttled both barred GPUs and apparently inside information to China, another with an Nvidia VP, plus at least a couple others he fessed up to. Oh, and he lied about them until he couldn’t anymore. Any semblance of corporate governance and ethics — at Nvidia and everywhere else by example — is utterly torched.

Hey, if you think that’s a buying opportunity, I’ve got some high-end GPUs in Singapore to sell you. Anyway, let’s move on before I tell you what I really think.

Paul Gillin dove into why open-weight AI models that enterprises can tailor to their specific needs are taking off this year. “The shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management,” he notes. “Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task.”

Last week Palo Alto Networks said it will acquire Applied Compute for $4.5 billion. This week was CrowdStrike’s turn, as it pulled the trigger on buying Zscaler for a pretty stunning $44 billion. As AI makes cyberattacks far easier and more numerous, it seems a sure bet that today’s rickety cybersecurity industry with hundred of point products won’t stand.

AI continues to be a big driver of upside earnings surprises, but investors increasingly wary of AI spending are all over the place. Dell in particular more than doubled its revenue, only to see its shares go nowhere Wednesday, while HP got hit by the PC slowdown but saw its shares rise more than 12%. Likewise, HPE’s stock slid despite an upbeat forecast.

Next week, look for earnings from Salesforce, Snowflake, UiPath, Marvell, MongoDB, NetApp, Okta and more.

But the big news next week will be AWS re:Invent, which customarily releases dozens of new services at its re:Invent conference in Las Vegas. SiliconANGLE, theCUBE Research, theCUBE, along with tens of thousands of attendees, will be onsite and we’ll have all the news, analysis and interviews.

#5372. Microsoft’s Brad Smith on Trump’s data center tax threat: ‘You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith said the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he said most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from New Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which says it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

His reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu

He gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he said. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

His one example was an unnamed company that wants to build in Finland. Google announced a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, said he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, said he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a big technology transfer offshore.”

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, said Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the company for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate company, and said Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith said Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

He put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the company “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered important.

Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He said the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he said much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.)

Smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5371. Estate Planning Attorney Jennifer McKenna Addresses Whether You Need a Trust or if a Will Is Enough

Jennifer McKenna explains how trusts and wills work together to support an estate planning strategy based on individual needs.

LEE'S SUMMIT, Mo., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Do you need a trust or is a will enough? A HelloNation article featuring insights from Estate Planning Attorney Jennifer McKenna of the Jennifer Ward McKenna, Attorney at Law in Lees Summit, Missouri, explains how trusts and wills serve different purposes within an estate planning strategy.

The article explains that many people begin estate planning by asking whether they need a trust or a will. The answer depends on factors such as family circumstances, financial goals, the types of assets they own, and how they want those assets managed after death. The article notes that both legal tools play important roles and understanding their differences helps individuals make informed decisions.

According to the article, a will is a legal document that explains how a person's property should be distributed after death. It also allows someone to name an executor to manage the estate and nominate guardians for minor children when necessary. The article describes a will as the foundation of many estate planning plans because it provides clear instructions and guidance for loved ones during a difficult time.

The HelloNation article also explains that a will always goes through the probate process after death. During probate, the court validates the will, oversees the payment of debts, and authorizes the distribution of assets. While probate is a routine legal process, the article notes that the timeline depends on the amount of assets administered through the will, the complexity of the estate, and state law. Some estates move through probate relatively quickly, while most require several months to resolve legal or administrative matters.

A trust serves a different purpose by allowing assets to be managed by a trustee for the benefit of designated beneficiaries. Unlike a will, many assets held in a properly funded trust can pass directly to beneficiaries without going through probate. The article explains that avoiding probate is one of the primary reasons some individuals include a trust as part of an overall estate planning strategy. It also notes that a trust can provide instructions for managing assets if the person creating the trust becomes unable to manage financial matters during their lifetime or when a beneficiary is unable to manage an inheritance effectively, such as a young child or an individual with special needs.

The article emphasizes that a trust is not automatically the right choice for every family. Establishing and maintaining a trust requires additional planning, and assets must be properly transferred into the trust for it to function as intended. If assets remain outside the trust, they may still be subject to probate. The article explains that understanding how a trust works is just as important as deciding whether to create one.

Rather than viewing these documents as alternatives, the article explains that a will and a trust often work together. A trust may be used to manage significant assets, while a will can address property that was not transferred into the trust and nominate guardians for minor children. According to the article, this combination creates a more complete estate planning approach that reflects a family's specific circumstances and long-term goals.

The article also notes that every estate is different, and no single solution works for everyone. Some individuals focus on protecting young children, while others are more concerned with managing business interests, real estate, or investment accounts. Estate planning allows legal documents to reflect those priorities instead of relying on general assumptions.

The article concludes that delaying estate planning because of uncertainty about choosing a trust or a will can leave important questions unanswered. Learning how a trust, a will, and probate work allows individuals to make informed decisions that fit their own circumstances. Whether someone ultimately chooses a will, a trust, or both, taking time to understand these legal tools can provide greater clarity and help protect loved ones in the future.

#5370. From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

The Sustainability Spotlight profiles individuals who are impacting the future of our planet by turning visionary climate tech concepts into real-world solutions.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm

Since Grant Canary launched his company a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

The company recently shifted again, adding a new line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary said, which benefits everyone.

Just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

High school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the issues.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

When I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there quickly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

That ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

My personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally important: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [New York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do big things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

In the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

My hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as big an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

Data and science guide us. Passion and invention drive us. We work backward from ambitious targets because that’s where progress happens, bringing innovation to the planet’s biggest challenges. Every package delivered, every data center powered, every product designed is an opportunity to make tomorrow better—and we share what we learn to help accelerate collective climate action.

#5368. Amazon is buying Decart’s AI chip software for a reported $7.5B and bringing its founders aboard

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

Amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported.

The deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled plans to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.

“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy said on the company’s earnings call last month.

Amazon announced the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role.

Decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips, mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.

Decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition.

Decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported. Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

The deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes. The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported.

Amazon bought Annapurna, also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

Amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon said last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

The deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron, a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Decart drew interest from other big buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August, before it walked away in September. Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech, and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

“From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf said in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”

The deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

#5367. Bitcoin News: Swiss ETF Debut Meets $7B Options Expiry and US Strategic Reserve Push

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin is facing a crowded weekend as bearish options positioning collides with a new Swiss spot ETF and news on the US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve. Nearly $7 billion in Bitcoin options expire November 27, while traders have shifted heavily toward downside protection. Meanwhile, Switzerland’s first spot Bitcoin ETF begins trading, and Washington is moving legislation that could lock government-held BTC away for 20 years.

Bitcoin hasn’t found much footing near $60,000, and Friday’s massive options expiry could make matters worse. But the bearish mood contrasts with developments in institutional access and US crypto policy, creating a market that could swing sharply with sentiment changes.

Around $7 billion in Bitcoin options expire Friday on Deribit, with another $600 million in Ethereum contracts expiring alongside them. Bitcoin options positioning has shifted rather sharply since October, when traders were betting more heavily on a recovery toward $90,000 and $100,000.

The put-call open interest ratio has climbed to 0.81 across all expiries, compared with 0.55 ahead of October’s settlement. Friday’s contracts show a ratio of 0.89, reflecting growing demand for downside protection as Bitcoin trades around $59,000.

Deribit Chief Commercial Officer Jean-David Pequignot said positioning had changed considerably since October, with puts now concentrated at $60,000 and lower. He pointed to major defensive clusters around $60,000, $58,000, $50,000 and $40,000.

Implied volatility has also climbed. Deribit’s Bitcoin DVOL index, which measures expected volatility over the next 30 days, rose to around 55 from 38 in October. Near-term options are now commanding a higher premium than longer-dated contracts, suggesting traders expect turbulence in the coming weeks.

History, however, offers no clear bearish signal from expiry alone. Bitcoin finished higher in the week following seven of the past 12 monthly expiries, lower after four, and unchanged after one. The median absolute move was 2.15%, compared with 3.1% for ordinary seven-day periods.

Bitcoin’s institutional access is expanding even as traders brace for another volatile session. The Bitcoin Fund ETF, ticker BBIT, began trading on the SIX Swiss Exchange today, giving Swiss investors direct Bitcoin exposure through a regulated investment fund.

The fund launched with 350 BTC and charges a 0.19% annual expense ratio. Bitcoin is held in cold storage at Swiss bank AMINA, with the fund available in Swiss francs and US dollars through traditional securities accounts.

🇨🇭 Today, Bitcoin Fund ETF (BBIT) will list on SIX Swiss Exchange: Switzerland’s first and only FINMA-approved Bitcoin ETF.🕘 Trading opens at 9:00 CET (8:00 UTC)News announcement: https://t.co/N112jUZiUP*Switzerland only. Not for US persons. Capital at risk. pic.twitter.com/CJa7lkh3uT

This launch is unlikely to reverse Bitcoin’s price weakness overnight. But it shows institutional infrastructure continuing to grow while prices fall, potentially widening the investor base when market sentiment eventually improves.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

🇺🇸JUST IN: The US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill is now eligible for a full House vote, banning any $BTC sales for 20 YEARS.Under the bill, Reserve Bitcoin can't be "sold, swapped, auctioned, encumbered, or otherwise disposed of" for at least 20 years.The bill does not allow… pic.twitter.com/qJmsgFtpWX

The House Financial Services Committee advanced the American Reserve Modernization Act, H.R. 8957, which would establish the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve in federal law. The bill would prohibit reserve Bitcoin from being sold, swapped, auctioned, or otherwise disposed of for at least 20 years. It also requires federal agencies to provide the Treasury with an accounting of their Bitcoin and other digital asset holdings.

The legislation has now been formally reported to the House and placed on the Union Calendar, making it eligible for a floor vote. It has not yet passed Congress, but it is good news for Bitcoin holders nevertheless.

Bitcoin now has a near-term derivatives test and two longer-term developments running in its favor. Friday could expose just how pessimistic the market has become.

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 2:39 pmNovember 24, 2026 at 6:55 am

— Muralidhar Krishnaprasad has been named as vice president of analytics, storage and databases at Amazon Web Services, a role that reports to AWS CEO Matt Garman. Krishnaprasad, who goes by MK, left Salesforce after eight years. He was president and chief technology officer there, where he helped build the company’s agentic enterprise platform.

At AWS, he will lead an organization that unites Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3), database and analytics services.

“MK brings deep technical roots, a customer-obsessed mindset and experience building data platforms at global scale,” Garman said in an email to staff.

Earlier in his career, MK spent more than a decade each at Oracle and Microsoft.

— After more than 13 years at Microsoft, Bonnie McCracken has been named VP of strategy and chief technology officer communications. She was previously general manager of innovation and thought leadership communications.

— Skye Scofield, Pablo Beltran and Brent Echols left OpenAI roughly two months ago to launch a Seattle startup that is currently in stealth mode. Scofield served as chief of staff to OpenAI’s Vijaye Raji, CTO of applications. Beltran and Echols, both software engineers, were members of the company’s technical staff.

More recently, Brandon Zinn joined the stealth startup as head of sales. All four overlapped in earlier roles at Statsig. In a post today on LinkedIn, Zinn asked for leads with home services owners “who could use help getting more work or making the business easier to run.”

The team is working with business owners in “roofing, tree care, plumbing, HVAC, painting, etc. Especially teams of 3–15 people where a lot still falls directly on the owner,” Zinn said.

Beltran said in a separate post that the startup has passed $100,000 in annual recurring revenue and is rapidly developing its software.

— Portal Space Systems, a Bothell, Wash.-based space company, has appointed Egbert Maben as principal satellite guidance, navigation and control (GNC) engineer — the startup’s first dedicated GNC hire. Last month, Portal reached Earth orbit for the second time this year.

Maben joined from Blue Origin, where he was a leader in GNC and hardware integration and helped resolve mission-critical hardware failures. He also tackled assembly, integration and test, a process that verifies the performance of software and hardware components. He previously spent nearly two decades at Lockheed Martin.

Maben, the company notes, has been keeping bees since ninth grade. “The only thing that’s left to see is whether Egbert, like bees, will be using dance to communicate those directives to our spacecraft,” Portal said on LinkedIn.

— Seattle-based Yoodli has named Jessica Evans as its first mid-market sales leader.The startup recently expanded from helping people practice speeches, sales pitches and job interviews to providing corporate training across a wide range of skills. Evans joins from ClickUp.

— PATH, a Seattle-based global health nonprofit, has appointed three new board members:

— Ian McAllister joined Boston-based Toast as vice president of Product, Video AI, in October after the restaurant software company acquired Airloom AI, the Seattle-area startup he founded and led as CEO. A longtime Seattle tech GM and product leader, he spent 12 years at Amazon and also held leadership roles at Airbnb and Uber.

McAllister said the idea for Airloom came when his wife, Sara McAllister, asked him to pick a security camera system for Allister, the Mercer Island restaurant and cocktail bar she owns and runs as GM. McAllister started Airloom AI to help restaurants use their existing video to improve the guest experience and operations. At Toast, he’ll continue that effort by combining Airloom’s technology with Toast’s platform. He’s building out Toast’s Vision AI team by hiring for multiple Seattle-based and remote product, engineering and AI/ML roles.

#5364. From dorm delivery robots to real‑world video games, UW students show off inventions

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Grace Kaste on Nov 23, 2026 at 3:29 pmNovember 23, 2026 at 3:29 pm

Recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering. Jobs seem to be disappearing every day, while coursework can be done by chatbots.

But at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club showed that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create. If anything, it’s allowing them to build things they wouldn’t have been able to before.

“We’re seeing projects that normal college students would not be expected to make,” club co-president Leonard Paya said. “As AI becomes more advanced, you can see how fast they scale up their knowledge and execute on things that are truly amazing.”

CSEED, founded a few years ago and already one of UW’s largest clubs, supports aspiring software designers and engineers. It’s funded by the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, as well as venture capital firms such as AI House, Madrona and Pack Ventures. Its members have gone on to join startup incubators including Y Combinator, Z Fellows and Founders Inc.

Twice a year, CSEED accepts applications for its Buildspace cohort, a program for students with hardware, software or design pitches. Over six weeks, the cohort meets up for build sessions, and they also receive mentorship, supplies and AI credits. Demo Day on Nov. 17 at the UW’s Gates Center marked the conclusion of the sixth Buildspace cohort, with 30 inventions presented to 150 audience members.

“We’ve brought together curious and ambitious students from all backgrounds,” vice president Amy Lu said. “CSEED gives them the community to turn their ideas into reality.”

One of the most technically advanced ideas presented was DubDash, a fully autonomous robot for delivering food orders from the dining hall to dorms.

“The best part of this is that these people were all freshmen who hadn’t yet taken robotics classes,” Paya said. “Who would have thought that four freshmen could make a fully fledged robot in six weeks?”

According to junior and Buildspace co-director Talal Kheiry, that’s a testament to AI. Buildspace members receive AI credits, which Kheiry said have changed everything.

“AI helps guide them through the gritty parts of the project, so they can just focus on the creative parts without worrying about the technical stuff,” Kheiry said.

Other inventions offered a glimpse into what’s on students’ minds these days. From notification-silencing focus apps to social connectors and mental health education platforms, nearly half of them had to do with curbing the effects of social media.

“Social media isn’t social anymore,” Junaid Akhtar told the audience as he and his three team members presented. “It’s just a place to see media. Our goal is to make social media bring people together again.”

His team’s presentation was the audience’s favorite: a satirical pitch for a platform they call FeedPicks, which creates live ranked prediction markets of friends’ social media feeds. Their demo won an award for “best energy” at the end of the night.

Other inventions sought to get users off their screens altogether. Joe Chae, a freshman at the Allen School, presented Pidgin, a Tinder-style app that helps users who want to practice each other’s languages to meet up in real life.

“I came to UW hoping to meet some Korean international students here and learn to speak Korean with my relatives, but I didn’t meet anyone,” Chae said. “So I thought, what if I made an app that could help me find someone who speaks Korean natively and wants to learn English?”

Also focused on the real world was Sasha Bogatirev’s Hadden Cybernetics. Bogatirev built a wearable gaming console that takes in information from a user’s environment and turns it into a game.

“The person has to pay attention to their surroundings,” Bogatirev said. “The idea is to prompt the imagination as much as possible for someone to experience another world.”

His prototype used the ESP32-S3 microcontroller to render the visuals onto wearable glasses. An nRF chip on the wristband takes in scripted gestures, which he trained to turn a player’s gestures into shields, lightning strikes and fireballs. Next, he plans to add haptics using hardware supplied by CSEED.

Andrew Edwards also built a video game accessory: cStar, which is an open source, low-cost console that can play a game on any TV screen by loading it onto an SD card and popping it into a 3D-printed box. Inside that box is a microcontroller like you’d find inside a stopwatch or a microwave, unlike the highly complicated circuitry used by an Xbox or PlayStation.

“We were able to squeeze HDMI video out of the microcontroller, which allows us to show 2D and 3D graphics on a home television set,” Edwards said. “Since the games are based on standard SD cards, a curious programmer can just write software on the computer, stick it onto an SD card, put it in the console and you’re ready to play.”

Other notable inventions presented at Demo Day:

This cohort was their largest and most competitive yet. Next up, under the guidance of club advisor and Allen School professor Kurtis Heimerl, CSEED is looking to expand. They’ve started hosting build sessions every Saturday that are open to non-students.

To do that, they’ll need to fundraise. According to CSEED co-president Benya Vahdat, they’ve already used up their Allen School allotment for the year, and they’re now in the process of raising money from donors. They recently incorporated as CSEED Foundation and received nonprofit status in Washington state.

“We want to grow this mentality of building, and maybe expand across campuses not just in Washington but across the country,” Vahdat said. “Maybe even globally.”

#5363. Dua Lipa defined internet cool. In a $44 billion creator economy, her successor may be harder to buy

Being the internet’s cool girl takes surprising work for someone who’s supposed to make it look effortless. She knows about the hole-in-the-wall restaurant before the line wraps around the block, has a vacation wardrobe worth taking notes on, and somehow finds time to read the book everyone will be talking about in six months.

Few have mastered that balancing act as well as Dua Lipa. The Grammy-winning pop star has become as much an inspiration for where to vacation, what to read, and where to eat as for what to listen to.

She interviews authors like Margaret Atwood for her book club, shares cultural recommendations through her lifestyle platform, Service95, and is a fixture in the fashion world.

But after years of celebrities turning their personalities into businesses and influencers making nearly every aspect of their lives shoppable, the economics of being cool may be changing. Being everywhere may no longer make someone worth following, which poses a slight problem for an industry that makes money off visibility.

U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion this year, more than triple the $13.9 billion spent in 2021, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. But even as brands pour more money into the creator economy, younger consumers are growing weary of its biggest stars.

A July survey of 13- to 39-year-olds from youth research firm YPulse found that 62% are tired of seeing the same big names everywhere, while 73% trust smaller creators more than big influencers.

“You can pay for attention, but you can’t buy cultural credibility or this idea of being cool,” Izzy Farmiloe, global head of strategy and growth at Dazed Studio, the agency arm of youth culture and fashion publisher Dazed Media, told Fortune.

Long before Instagram gave celebrities a place to document their breakfast, much of the fascination with the cool girl came from how little the public knew about her.

In a November essay for his newsletter, Considered Chaos, brand strategist Eugene Healey explained how each generation’s cool girl was shaped by the media of her time. Kate Moss had fashion magazines, the Olsen twins had the paparazzi, and Alexa Chung had fashion blogs and street-style photographers.

Social media brought audiences closer to the women they admired, making relatability an asset for personalities like Emma Chamberlain. As algorithms began serving up content based on people’s interests rather than simply who they followed, celebrities also had more reason to venture beyond the industries that made them famous.

“Dua Lipa was made for the feed,” Healey wrote.

Her friendship with designer Simon Porte Jacquemus might draw in fashion enthusiasts, while her book club could introduce her to someone who has never listened to Future Nostalgia. Each new audience offers another opportunity to make money beyond selling records and concert tickets.

It’s a business model that has become increasingly familiar, with celebrities launching beauty brands, starting newsletters, and inviting followers into their kitchens. Somewhere along the way, having a favorite lip gloss became an opportunity to launch a cosmetics company.

The trouble with making a living off being cool is that the more people see someone being paid to recommend things, the harder it becomes to tell what she actually likes. Even the seemingly casual Instagram photo dump, filled with blurry pictures and half-eaten meals, can be as carefully curated as the polished posts it was meant to replace.

For Jenna Drenten, a marketing professor at Loyola University Chicago, the problem lies in the very nature of an influencer’s job. “They are expected to sell what is popular, but also expected to discover what’s new,” Drenten told Fortune.

Drenten pointed to BookTok, where recommending a novel outside the usual bestseller rotation can set a creator apart. If enough people take her advice, however, the book becomes just another BookTok sensation, losing some of the very appeal that made it worth recommending in the first place.

Brands risk falling into the same trap. Farmiloe has seen companies chase the same trends and hire the same talent in their pursuit of relevance, spending money only to end up looking more like one another.

“I actually think silence can often be a stronger strategy now,” Farmiloe said.

Trying too hard to look polished may also backfire for brands, especially as artificial intelligence makes it easier to produce everything from flawless images to cultural recommendations. “To sort of show mistakes is a way of proving that a human has made something,” Farmiloe said, adding that even typos have become chic.

Healey identified three potential successors to the Dua Lipa era: the obsessive, who knows a particular subject inside and out; the ghost, whose reputation spreads without constantly posting; and the host, who brings people together in real life.

He argued that the three share expertise and charisma that are hard to fake at a moment when faking has never been easier. If the next dominant medium is an AI model that can summarize the world’s knowledge on demand, Healey wrote, cool becomes whatever can’t be summarized.

For brands accustomed to measuring influence in followers, likes, and views, the next cool girl may be much harder to price. Drenten sees growing appeal in people who can offer something beyond a product recommendation, whether it’s a longtime librarian who can introduce readers to literature they might never have discovered on their own or someone who brings strangers together outside the confines of their carefully curated feeds.

As going out becomes increasingly expensive, Farmiloe sees an opportunity for brands to help create those experiences. She pointed to Reference Point, a London library, bookshop, and bar that doubles as a gathering place for chess, poetry, and jazz.

Rather than paying someone to talk about a brand, companies could give people a place to spend time together.

“Instead of just getting noticed, how do you get people to care or actually like engage or spend time with your brand?” Farmiloe said.

Tatiana Sataua is a News Fellow at Fortune covering business, technology, AI, and consumer culture.

#5362. Copilot without M365, and more news you didn’t hear (but maybe should have) at Microsoft Ignite

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 24, 2026 at 6:44 amNovember 24, 2026 at 6:44 am

Many Microsoft business customers are still wading through the session slide decks and “Book of News” collection of product and strategy announcements from Microsoft’s Ignite confab last week. But not all the new goodies announced there (or simultaneous with this year’s Microsoft Ignite show, which kicked off Nov. 17) might have made it onto everyone’s radar.

Microsoft’s curated Ignite keynote and session spotlights were, unsurprisingly, dedicated to Microsoft AI in all its guises — Copilot, the Microsoft IQ intelligence platforms and Agent 365. But there was some other important news last week that Microsoft customers could find equally, if not more, interesting and useful.

Among my picks for the “make sure you didn’t miss this” list:

Copilot without the M365 subscription prerequisite arrives next week: Despite a LOT of talk about Copilot, “a new OS for work,” Microsoft didn’t mention anything at all during Ignite about a new purchasing option for Copilot that is set to go live on Dec. 1. Starting then, Microsoft will offer a version of Copilot to small business and enterprise customers without the current prerequisite of having a certain paid Microsoft 365 plan.

For a flat fee of $21 per user per month for small businesses and $30 per user per month for enterprise customers (before discounts), users will be able to buy this new standalone Copilot offering, as Microsoft quietly announced back in October on its Partner Center site.

Currently, to buy Copilot, business customers need to have purchased a qualifying Microsoft 365 subscription plan before they shell out even more money for Copilot. Because of this requirement, Microsoft isn’t competitive price-wise when pitted against OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude entry-level business tiers.

The new offer is for new customers buying through any of Microsoft’s channels, including its Cloud Solution Provider program, across commercial, education, government and nonprofit sectors.

I’ve got a lot of questions about this new offer, including where Copilot chats are stored and how/if customers will get some kind of access to the Microsoft IQ technology that underlies Copilot and is positioned as its secret sauce if they don’t have a Microsoft 365 subscription. I’ve asked Microsoft, but no word back so far.

Azure Linux 4.0 is now ready for prime time: Announced on the same day Ignite kicked off (but without a mention during the conference), Microsoft’s own commercial Linux distribution, Azure Linux 4.0, is now generally available.

The 4.0 release is interesting for a few reasons. First, it is the first release of Azure Linux — formerly known as Common Base Linux (CBL)-Mariner — designed as a general-purpose server OS for customer virtual machines, and it is based on the Fedora Linux stack. Checking off the requisite AI box, Azure Linux 4.0 is “purpose-built for cloud native and AI workloads,” as Microsoft said back in May.

Microsoft officials have said two-thirds of customer cores in Azure run Linux (not Windows Server). Microsoft has acknowledged the platforms running Microsoft 365, GitHub and OpenAI’s ChatGPT “all sit on Linux foundations.”

Microsoft has supported a wide variety of Linux distributions on Azure for years but never made its own available for commercial use by customers and partners until now.

Windows Server 2028 is in the works: Yes, another on-premises version of Windows Server is coming. Christened Windows Server 2028, the next release, likely to debut in late 2027, is now in public preview.

Microsoft mentioned Server 2028 in its Book of News and in passing in some sessions, but it was not positioned as a top-tier announcement.

The 2028 release includes some expected and a few surprise features, such as making 32-bit app support an optional component rather than installing it by default. That change, along with a hardened Server Core configuration included by default, is designed to improve the security of the platform from the get-go. But they may present potential backward-compatibility risks.

Microsoft is positioning Server 2028 similarly to the way it has been pushing Windows client lately: as a way to run AI workloads more cheaply because they can run locally. The “unmetered intelligence” pitch strikes again.

Sure, Microsoft can’t make every announcement a centerpiece in a two-plus-hour (waah!) opening keynote. But sometimes, hidden gems deserve their moments in the sun. Or pouring rain …

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

Learn more about the technology making it all work.

#5361. How Kohl's Cash rules decide what a $10-per-$50 reward is worth

Kohl's Cash pays $10 for every $50 spent in one purchase. See how 7 rules on spend, delivery, use, exclusions and returns affect it.

Credit: Mike Mozart / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

Retailers offering freebies and rebates this holiday weekend expect something in return: a trip to the store and more spending once the shopper is inside. In an ICSC survey reported by TheStreet, 49% of shoppers say they're worried about affording holiday gifts, and 68% say discounts and promotions will get them shopping in stores more. A holiday reward aimed at these shoppers is a bargain with two sides, and the retailer has already set the terms.

Kohl's $KSS is offering its own reward over the holiday weekend while fewer people come into its stores. Its store visits are down 1.4%, according to Placer.ai figures, so any offer that brings shoppers back has clear value. Its standard reward, Kohl's Cash, arrives only after a purchase as store currency, and the rules attached to it decide how much of the printed amount a shopper actually keeps.

Kohl's lays out its Kohl's Cash rules and the giveaways it ran over the Nov. 27–29 holiday weekend, from how the qualifying spend is counted to what a return does to rewards already issued. Shoppers who plan their purchases around these rules keep more of the reward than shoppers who don't.

Kohl's $KSS Cash rewards a shopper according to the size of one purchase: $15 back for each $50 spent in a single transaction during the Black Friday event. The reward rises only in $50 steps, so a basket that stops short of the next step earns nothing for the extra items in it. That gives shoppers a reason to add one more item to reach the next step.

Kohl's paid $10 for every $50 during its Deal Days, Oct. 6–8, 2026, so the rate changes from event to event. Shoppers should check the current rate before planning a purchase around it.

Kohl's sets the promotion's hours in Central Time, so a shopper in a western time zone who waits until the last evening by their own clock may find the offer has already ended.

The rate pays off best for shoppers who were going to spend that much at Kohl's

The spending that counts toward Kohl's $KSS Cash is the total after markdowns and coupons, with tax and shipping left out. Every coupon a shopper uses also lowers the amount Kohl's counts, so anyone aiming for the threshold should add up the merchandise after discounts before reaching the register.

Kohl's also counts each purchase on its own, so two smaller orders placed over the weekend don't add together toward the threshold. A shopper who usually spreads gift buying across several trips can reach the threshold more easily by pulling those purchases into one larger order.

Kohl's $KSS, not the shopper, decides the order of discounts at checkout, and the dollar-off value of Kohl's Cash comes off before any percent-off coupon. The coupon's percentage then applies to the smaller total, so a shopper who stacks a coupon on top of Kohl's Cash should expect the combined savings to come in a little lower than the two added together.

Spending Kohl's Cash doesn't require a second trip to the store. Kohl's accepts the reward on its website as well as at its stores and kiosks, and each of those options still ends in a

A Kohl's $KSS Cash voucher stays tied to the purchase that earned it. A shopper who brings an item back may get a smaller refund than expected, and Kohl's may also adjust Kohl's Cash it has already issued.

The rule covers items bought with Kohl's Cash as well as items that earned it, and Kohl's gives no formula for how much a return takes back. Anyone unsure about a gift, a size or a color should treat the Kohl's Cash it earned as provisional until they're sure they'll keep the item.

A shopper doesn't use Kohl's $KSS Cash to lower the bill for the purchase that earns it. Kohl's issues the reward after the sale as a separate voucher, by email, printed on the receipt or inside the Kohl's app, and each of those is something the shopper has to keep track of until the next trip.

The sensible habit is to ask at the register how the reward was sent, then save that email, tuck the receipt somewhere safe or check the app before leaving the parking lot.

A shopper collects the rebate only by still holding it when it's time to spend.

A shopper can lose some vouchers entirely. Kohl's applies forfeiture to promotional vouchers under the terms of each offer, not to all Kohl's Cash, so a shopper should read the terms of any voucher that came from a promotion.

Kohl's Cash can be spent anywhere Kohl's sells, but promotional vouchers come with their own fine print.

Gift cards, taxes, shipping and fees are excluded from both earning and redeeming Kohl's $KSS Cash. Gift cards matter most to holiday buyers: a gift card purchase earns nothing toward the reward, and a shopper can't convert Kohl's Cash into a gift card.

Even when Kohl's Cash covers every item in the bag, the shopper still pays these costs in real money.

Keep the item before you spend the reward it earned.

Each Kohl's $KSS store handed its first 200 customers on Friday a voucher worth between $5 and $100, no purchase required. Those vouchers are Kohl's Cash, according to NBC 5 Dallas-Fort Worth, so even the free prize can be spent only at Kohl's.

Stores opened at 5 a.m. on Friday, Nov. 27, and only shoppers near the front of the line got a voucher. Kohl's followed on Saturday, Nov. 28, with a second giveaway of Sephora coupons.

Kohl's spreads its giveaway across many shoppers but keeps the top prize modest. At Academy Sports + Outdoors, only 100 shoppers per store get a voucher, but those run from $20 up to $500. The one Kohl's giveaway paid in money a shopper can spend anywhere is the $10,000 cash sweepstakes, and entering offers only a chance at it.

What Kohl's gives away for free this weekend is mostly built to come back to Kohl's.
